lessons.title: Introduction to Limits
lessons.intro: A limit describes what value a function approaches as its input approaches some point — whether or not the function actually reaches that value. Limits are the foundation everything in calculus is built on.
concepts: Notation — lim x→a f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x gets arbitrarily close to a (with x ≠ a).
Approach from both sides — the limit exists only when the values approached from the left and from the right agree.
The function value doesn't matter — f(a) can be different from the limit, or even undefined, while the limit still exists.
Estimating — you can estimate a limit from a table of values or a graph before computing it exactly.

example.q: Find lim x→2 (x² − 4)/(x − 2).
steps: Direct substitution gives (4 − 4)/(2 − 2) = 0/0, which is undefined — but that says nothing about the limit.
Factor the numerator: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2).
Cancel (x − 2) — allowed because in the limit x approaches 2 but never equals 2: the expression equals x + 2.
Now substitute: lim x→2 (x + 2) = 4.

practice.q: Estimate lim x→0 (sin x)/x from values at x = ±0.1, ±0.01.
practice.a: The values approach 1, so the limit is 1 — one of the most important limits in calculus.

practice.q: Find lim x→5 (x − 5)/(x − 5).
practice.a: For every x ≠ 5 the expression equals 1, so the limit is 1 (even though the function is undefined at x = 5).

lessons.takeaway: A limit is about approach, not arrival: simplify the expression first, then substitute.

lessons.title: Limit Laws
lessons.intro: Once a few basic limits are known, the limit laws let you build the limit of a complicated expression from the limits of its pieces — sums, products, quotients, powers, and roots.
concepts: Sum and product laws — the limit of a sum (or product) is the sum (or product) of the limits, when they exist.
Quotient law — the limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the denominator's limit is not 0.
Direct substitution for polynomials and rational functions — if f is a polynomial, or rational with a nonzero denominator at a, then lim x→a f(x) = f(a).
Squeeze theorem — if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and both outer limits equal L, then f's limit is L too.

example.q: Find lim x→3 (2x² − 5x + 1).
steps: This is a polynomial, so direct substitution applies.
Substitute x = 3: 2(3²) − 5(3) + 1.

practice.q: Find lim x→−1 (x² + 3x)/(x + 2).
Use the squeeze theorem to show lim x→0 x² sin(1/x) = 0.
practice.a: Since −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x² and both bounds → 0, the limit is 0.

lessons.takeaway: Try direct substitution first; reach for factoring, rationalizing, or the squeeze theorem only when substitution gives 0/0 or fails.

lessons.title: One-Sided Limits and Infinite Limits
lessons.intro: Sometimes a function behaves differently on the two sides of a point, or grows without bound near it. One-sided limits and infinite limits describe both situations precisely.
concepts: One-sided limits — lim x→a⁻ f(x) uses values left of a; lim x→a⁺ f(x) uses values right of a.
Existence test — the two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
Infinite limits — lim x→a f(x) = ∞ means f(x) grows beyond every bound as x approaches a; the line x = a is then a vertical asymptote.
Sign analysis — for rational functions, check the sign of numerator and denominator on each side to decide between +∞ and −∞.

example.q: Find the one-sided limits of f(x) = |x|/x at x = 0 and decide whether lim x→0 f(x) exists.
steps: For x > 0, |x| = x, so f(x) = x/x = 1. The right-hand limit is 1.
For x < 0, |x| = −x, so f(x) = −x/x = −1. The left-hand limit is −1.
Left (−1) ≠ right (1), so the two-sided limit does not exist.
example.a: Left limit −1, right limit 1; the two-sided limit does not exist.

practice.q: Find lim x→1⁺ 1/(x − 1) and lim x→1⁻ 1/(x − 1).
practice.a: +∞ from the right (small positive denominator) and −∞ from the left (small negative denominator). x = 1 is a vertical asymptote.

practice.q: Find lim x→2 1/(x − 2)².
practice.a: The denominator is a small positive number on both sides, so the limit is +∞.

lessons.takeaway: At a suspicious point, always test both sides separately — and let the signs tell you +∞ versus −∞.

lessons.title: Limits at Infinity
lessons.intro: Limits at infinity describe a function's end behavior: what happens as x grows without bound in either direction. They reveal horizontal asymptotes and are the first step toward improper integrals.
concepts: Notation — lim x→∞ f(x) = L means f(x) settles toward L as x grows; the line y = L is a horizontal asymptote.
Key fact — lim x→∞ 1/xʳ = 0 for any r > 0. Small-over-large terms vanish.
Rational function rule — compare degrees: numerator degree smaller → limit 0; equal degrees → ratio of leading coefficients; numerator larger → infinite limit.
Technique — divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of x in the denominator.

example.q: Find lim x→∞ (3x² + 2x)/(x² − 5).
steps: Divide top and bottom by x²: (3 + 2/x)/(1 − 5/x²).
As x → ∞, 2/x → 0 and 5/x² → 0.
The limit is (3 + 0)/(1 − 0) = 3.
example.a: 3 — the line y = 3 is a horizontal asymptote.

practice.q: Find lim x→∞ (7x − 1)/(2x² + 3).
practice.a: 0 — the denominator's degree is higher.

practice.q: Find lim x→−∞ (4x³ + x)/(2x³ − 5).
practice.a: 2 — equal degrees, ratio of leading coefficients 4/2.

lessons.takeaway: For rational functions at infinity, only the highest-degree terms matter in the long run.

lessons.title: Continuity
lessons.intro: A function is continuous at a point when you can draw it there without lifting your pen: the limit exists, the function is defined, and the two agree. Continuity is what makes the big theorems of calculus work.
concepts: Definition — f is continuous at a when (1) f(a) is defined, (2) lim x→a f(x) exists, (3) the limit equals f(a).
Types of discontinuity — removable (a hole: limit exists but value differs or is missing), jump (one-sided limits differ), infinite (vertical asymptote).
Continuity on an interval — continuous at every interior point, and one-sided continuous at the endpoints.

Building continuous functions — sums, products, quotients (nonzero denominator), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous wherever defined.

example.q: Show that f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, with f(3) = 5, is not continuous at 3, and classify the discontinuity.
steps: Factor: (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = x + 3 for x ≠ 3, so lim x→3 f(x) = 6.
But f(3) = 5 ≠ 6 — condition (3) fails.
Because the limit exists and only the value is wrong, the discontinuity is removable: redefining f(3) = 6 would fix it.

practice.q: Where is f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 1) discontinuous?
practice.a: Factor first: (x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = 1/(x − 1) for x ≠ −1. So x = −1 is a removable discontinuity (a hole — the factor cancels), and x = 1 is an infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote).

practice.q: For what k is f(x) = x² for x ≤ 2, kx − 2 for x > 2, continuous at 2?
practice.a: Need 2k − 2 = 4, so k = 3.

lessons.takeaway: Continuity = limit exists + value exists + they match. Name which condition fails and you know the type of break.

lessons.title: Intermediate Value Theorem
lessons.intro: The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) says a continuous function on an interval takes every value between its endpoint values. It sounds obvious — and it is the standard way to prove equations have solutions.
concepts: Statement — if f is continuous on [a, b] and N is any number between f(a) and f(b), then some c in (a, b) has f(c) = N.
Root-finding use — if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, IVT guarantees a root (a c with f(c) = 0) between them.
Continuity is essential — a function with a jump can skip values, so IVT does not apply.
Bisection — IVT justifies repeatedly halving an interval that brackets a root to approximate it.

example.q: Show that x³ + x − 1 = 0 has a solution between 0 and 1.
steps: Let f(x) = x³ + x − 1. Polynomials are continuous everywhere.
f(0) = −1 (negative) and f(1) = 1 + 1 − 1 = 1 (positive).
0 lies between −1 and 1, so by the IVT some c in (0, 1) has f(c) = 0.
(Numerically, c ≈ 0.682.)
example.a: A root exists in (0, 1), guaranteed by the IVT.

practice.q: Show cos x = x has a solution in (0, 1).
practice.a: Let g(x) = cos x − x. g(0) = 1 > 0 and g(1) ≈ 0.540 − 1 < 0, so IVT gives a root in (0, 1).

practice.q: Why can't IVT be used on f(x) = 1/x over [−1, 1] to claim a root?
practice.a: f is not continuous on [−1, 1] — it is undefined and unbounded at 0 — and indeed it never equals 0.

lessons.takeaway: Opposite signs at the ends of an interval + continuity = a root in between. IVT proves existence, not the value.

lessons.title: Derivatives and Rates of Change
lessons.intro: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change. It turns 'how fast on average' into 'how fast right now' — velocity from position, slope from secant lines.
concepts: Average rate of change — (f(a + h) − f(a))/h is the slope of the secant line through two points of the graph.
Instantaneous rate / derivative — f′(a) = lim h→0 (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, the slope of the tangent line at a.
Velocity — if s(t) is position, average velocity is Δs/Δt and instantaneous velocity is s′(t).
The limit must exist — corners, cusps, and vertical tangents are points where the derivative fails to exist.

example.q: Using the definition, find the derivative of f(x) = x² at x = 3.
steps: Form the difference quotient: ((3 + h)² − 3²)/h = (9 + 6h + h² − 9)/h = (6h + h²)/h.
Simplify (h ≠ 0): 6 + h.
Take the limit as h → 0: 6.
example.a: f′(3) = 6 — the tangent line to y = x² at x = 3 has slope 6.

practice.q: A ball's height is s(t) = 16t − 4t² metres. Find its average velocity on [1, 2] and instantaneous velocity at t = 1.
practice.a: Average: (s(2) − s(1))/1 = (16 − 12) = 4 m/s. Instantaneous: s′(t) = 16 − 8t, so s′(1) = 8 m/s.

practice.q: Why does f(x) = |x| have no derivative at 0?
practice.a: The difference quotient is −1 from the left and +1 from the right, so the limit does not exist — the graph has a corner.

lessons.takeaway: Derivative = limit of the difference quotient. Every shortcut rule later is this limit, pre-computed.

lessons.title: The Derivative as a Function
lessons.intro: Instead of differentiating at one point at a time, we can differentiate a whole function at once: f′ is itself a function, giving the slope of f at every point.
concepts: Definition — f′(x) = lim h→0 (f(x + h) − f(x))/h, wherever this limit exists.
Notations — f′(x), dy/dx, Df(x), and y′ all mean the same thing; Leibniz's dy/dx suggests a ratio and guides the chain rule.
Graphical link — f′ > 0 where f rises, f′ < 0 where f falls, f′ = 0 at peaks, troughs, and flat spots.
Differentiability implies continuity — if f′(a) exists then f is continuous at a; the converse is false (|x| at 0 is continuous but not differentiable).

example.q: Use the definition to find f′(x) for f(x) = x², and evaluate f′(−1), f′(0), f′(2).
steps: Difference quotient: ((x + h)² − x²)/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h.
Limit as h → 0: f′(x) = 2x.
Evaluate: f′(−1) = −2 (falling), f′(0) = 0 (flat — the vertex), f′(2) = 4 (rising steeply).

practice.q: Find f′(x) for f(x) = 1/x using the definition.
Sketch the sign of f′ for a function that falls until x = 2, then rises.

lessons.takeaway: f′ is a machine: feed it any x, get the slope of f at that x. Its sign chart is the story of where f rises and falls.

lessons.title: Differentiation Rules
lessons.intro: Nobody computes limits by definition for every derivative. The power, product, and quotient rules turn differentiation into algebra.
concepts: Power rule — d/dx xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹, for any real n. Constants have derivative 0; constant multiples and sums differentiate term by term.
Exponential — d/dx eˣ = eˣ (the function that is its own derivative); d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a.
Product rule — (fg)′ = f′g + fg′. Order matters: derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times derivative of the second.
Quotient rule — (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g². The numerator starts with the derivative of the top.

example.q: Differentiate f(x) = (x² + 1)(3x − 2) with the product rule.
steps: Let u = x² + 1 (u′ = 2x) and v = 3x − 2 (v′ = 3).
Expand: 6x² − 4x + 3x² + 3 = 9x² − 4x + 3.
Check by expanding first: f = 3x³ − 2x² + 3x − 2, whose derivative is 9x² − 4x + 3. ✓

practice.q: Differentiate y = (x + 1)/(x − 1).
Differentiate y = 4x⁵ − 3x² + 7eˣ.
practice.a: y′ = 20x⁴ − 6x + 7eˣ.

lessons.takeaway: Identify the structure first — sum, product, or quotient — then apply exactly one rule at a time.

lessons.title: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
lessons.intro: Two limits power everything here: lim h→0 (sin h)/h = 1 and lim h→0 (cos h − 1)/h = 0. From them come the derivatives of all six trigonometric functions.
concepts: The two key derivatives — d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = −sin x (note the minus sign).
Tangent — d/dx tan x = sec² x, derived from sin/cos with the quotient rule.
The rest — d/dx sec x = sec x tan x; d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x; d/dx cot x = −csc² x. The 'co-' functions carry the minus signs.
Radians only — these formulas are true when x is measured in radians; that is why calculus always uses radians.

example.q: Differentiate y = x sin x.
steps: This is a product: u = x (u′ = 1), v = sin x (v′ = cos x).
y′ = u′v + uv′ = 1·sin x + x·cos x.
example.a: y′ = sin x + x cos x

practice.q: Differentiate y = tan x − x.
practice.a: y′ = sec² x − 1 = tan² x.

practice.q: Find the slope of y = cos x at x = π.
practice.a: y′ = −sin x, so at π the slope is −sin π = 0 — a horizontal tangent at the trough.

lessons.takeaway: Memorize sin and cos cold; derive tan from the quotient rule when you need it, and remember: co-functions get the minus.

lessons.title: The Chain Rule
lessons.intro: Most real functions are compositions — a function inside another function. The chain rule is how you differentiate them: derivative of the outer (at the inner) times derivative of the inner.
concepts: Statement — if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). In Leibniz form: dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx).
Outside-in — differentiate the outermost function first, leaving the inside untouched, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
Generalized power rule — d/dx [g(x)]ⁿ = n[g(x)]ⁿ⁻¹ · g′(x), the chain rule's most common special case.
Nesting — three or more layers just keep multiplying: one factor per layer.

example.q: Differentiate y = (3x² + 1)⁵.
steps: Outer: u⁵ with u = 3x² + 1. Derivative of the outer at the inner: 5(3x² + 1)⁴.
Inner derivative: d/dx (3x² + 1) = 6x.
Multiply: y′ = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ · 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.

practice.q: Differentiate y = sin(x²).
practice.a: y′ = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²).

practice.q: Differentiate (a) y = e^(3x) and (b) y = √(x² + 4).
practice.a: (a) 3e^(3x) — the chain rule contributes the factor 3 from the exponent. (b) y′ = (1/(2√(x² + 4)))·2x = x/√(x² + 4).

lessons.takeaway: Peel the function like an onion — outermost layer first, and never forget to multiply by the derivative of what was inside.

lessons.title: Implicit Differentiation
lessons.intro: Many curves are not given as y = f(x) at all — x² + y² = 25 describes a circle. Implicit differentiation finds dy/dx anyway, by differentiating both sides with respect to x and treating y as a function of x.
concepts: The method — differentiate every term with respect to x; whenever you differentiate a y-term, multiply by dy/dx (the chain rule). Then solve for dy/dx.
d/dx y² = 2y · dy/dx, not 2y — the most common place students drop the dy/dx factor.
Product terms with x and y — like xy — need the product rule, which introduces both y and x·dy/dx terms.
Tangent lines — dy/dx at a specific point (x₀, y₀) on the curve gives the tangent slope there.

example.q: For x² + y² = 25, find dy/dx and the tangent slope at (3, 4).
steps: Differentiate both sides: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0.
Solve: dy/dx = −x/y.
At (3, 4): slope = −3/4. (Check geometrically: the radius to (3, 4) has slope 4/3, and the tangent is perpendicular — negative reciprocal −3/4. ✓)

practice.q: Find dy/dx for x² + xy + y² = 7.
practice.a: 2x + y + x·dy/dx + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y).

practice.q: Find dy/dx for sin y = x.
practice.a: cos y · dy/dx = 1, so dy/dx = 1/cos y = sec y.

lessons.takeaway: Differentiate everything in x, tag every y-derivative with dy/dx, then do algebra. Geometry (like the circle's radius) is a great check.

lessons.title: Related Rates
lessons.intro: In a related rates problem, several quantities change together in time and are linked by an equation. Differentiate the link with respect to time and the rates become linked too.
concepts: Setup — identify the quantities, the rate you know, and the rate you want; write an equation connecting the quantities (geometry is the usual source).
Differentiate in t — every variable that changes with time gets a d/dt factor via the chain rule (e.g. d/dt x² = 2x dx/dt).
Substitute numbers LAST — plug in the instant's values only after differentiating; substituting early turns variables into constants and destroys the rates.
Sign meaning — a negative rate means the quantity is decreasing; state direction in your answer.

example.q: A 10 ft ladder leans on a wall. The bottom slides away at 1 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is 6 ft from the wall?
steps: Let x = distance of the bottom from the wall, y = height of the top. Link: x² + y² = 10² = 100 (Pythagoras).
Differentiate in t: 2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt = 0.
At the instant: x = 6, so y = √(100 − 36) = 8; dx/dt = 1.
Solve: dy/dt = −(x/y) dx/dt = −(6/8)(1) = −0.75 ft/s.
example.a: The top slides down at 0.75 ft/s (the negative sign means y is decreasing).

practice.q: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast is the volume growing when r = 2 cm? (V = (4/3)πr³)
practice.a: dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt = 4π(4)(0.5) = 8π ≈ 25.1 cm³/s.

practice.q: For a cone being filled, which equation links V, r, h before differentiating?
practice.a: V = (1/3)πr²h — and if r and h are proportional (similar triangles from the cone's shape), eliminate one variable first.

lessons.takeaway: Equation first, differentiate in t second, numbers last. That order is the whole method.

lessons.title: Extrema on an Interval
lessons.intro: Extreme values are the largest and smallest outputs of a function. On a closed interval, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees they exist — and they can only occur at critical numbers or endpoints.
concepts: Extreme Value Theorem — a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.
Critical numbers — values c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist. Interior extrema can only occur there (Fermat's theorem).
Closed Interval Method — evaluate f at every critical number in the interval and at both endpoints; the biggest output is the absolute max, the smallest is the absolute min.
Local vs absolute — a local max is biggest in its neighbourhood; the absolute max is biggest on the whole interval, and often sits at an endpoint.

example.q: Find the absolute extrema of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [−2, 2].
steps: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), so critical numbers are x = −1 and x = 1 (both in the interval).
Evaluate: f(−1) = 2, f(1) = −2.
Compare all four values {2, −2, −2, 2}: maximum 2, minimum −2.
example.a: Absolute max 2 (at x = −1 and x = 2); absolute min −2 (at x = 1 and x = −2).

practice.q: Find the absolute extrema of f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 3].
practice.a: f′ = 2x − 4 = 0 at x = 2, f(2) = −4. Endpoints: f(0) = 0, f(3) = −3. Absolute min −4 at x = 2; absolute max 0 at x = 0.

practice.q: Why does the Closed Interval Method fail on an open interval (0, 2)?
practice.a: An open interval need not contain its extreme values — f(x) = x on (0, 2) has neither an absolute max nor min there.

lessons.takeaway: Candidates for absolute extrema = critical numbers + endpoints. Evaluate them all; never skip the endpoints.

lessons.title: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem
lessons.intro: These two theorems connect a function's average behaviour to its instantaneous behaviour: somewhere inside the interval, the tangent is parallel to the secant.
concepts: Rolle's theorem — if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then some c in (a, b) has f′(c) = 0.
Mean Value Theorem (MVT) — under the same continuity/differentiability conditions, some c has f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a): instantaneous rate equals average rate.
Hypotheses matter — one failed hypothesis (a corner, a jump) can destroy the conclusion.
Consequences — MVT is the engine behind the derivative tests, error bounds, and the fact that zero derivative everywhere forces a function to be constant.

example.q: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on [1, 3] and find the promised c.
steps: f is a polynomial: continuous and differentiable everywhere.
f(1) = 1 − 4 + 3 = 0 and f(3) = 9 − 12 + 3 = 0 — equal endpoint values ✓.
f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2, which lies in (1, 3).
example.a: c = 2, where the tangent is horizontal.

practice.q: Apply the MVT to f(x) = x² on [0, 2] and find c.
practice.a: Average rate = (4 − 0)/2 = 2. f′(c) = 2c = 2, so c = 1.

practice.q: Why does f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] have no c with f′(c) = 0 even though f(−1) = f(1)?
practice.a: f is not differentiable at 0, so Rolle's hypotheses fail — and indeed f′ is ±1 everywhere it exists, never 0.

lessons.takeaway: Equal endpoints force a flat tangent (Rolle); in general, somewhere the instantaneous rate exactly matches the average rate (MVT).

lessons.title: First Derivative Test
lessons.intro: The sign of f′ tells you where f climbs and where it falls. Where that sign changes at a critical number, you have found a local extremum — that is the first derivative test.
concepts: Sign chart — split the number line at critical numbers; test f′ at one sample point in each interval.
Rising/falling — f′ > 0 on an interval means f is increasing there; f′ < 0 means decreasing.
The test — at a critical number, + to − change in f′ means local max; − to + means local min; no sign change means neither.
Process — factor f′ fully: its factors' signs make the chart fast and reliable.

example.q: Classify the critical numbers of f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 9x.
steps: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1). Critical numbers: x = −1, x = 3.
Sign of f′: positive on (−∞, −1) [test −2: 3(−5)(−1) > 0], negative on (−1, 3) [test 0: −9 < 0], positive on (3, ∞).
At −1, f′ changes + to −: local max, f(−1) = −1 − 3 + 9 = 5.
At 3, f′ changes − to +: local min, f(3) = 27 − 27 − 27 = −27.
example.a: Local max 5 at x = −1; local min −27 at x = 3.

practice.q: Classify x = 0 for f(x) = x⁴.
practice.a: f′ = 4x³ changes − to + at 0, so x = 0 is a local (and absolute) min, f(0) = 0.

practice.q: Classify x = 0 for f(x) = x³.
practice.a: f′ = 3x² is positive on both sides — no sign change, so no extremum at 0 (it's a flat inflection point).

lessons.takeaway: Extrema live where f′ changes sign — not merely where f′ = 0.

lessons.title: Second Derivative Test
lessons.intro: The second derivative measures concavity — whether the graph cups upward or downward. At a critical number, concavity alone can classify the point, and where concavity flips you get inflection points.
concepts: Concavity — f′′ > 0: concave up (f′ increasing, graph holds water); f′′ < 0: concave down.
Inflection points — points where concavity changes and the graph has a tangent line.
Second derivative test — at a critical number c with f′(c) = 0: f′′(c) > 0 → local min; f′′(c) < 0 → local max; f′′(c) = 0 → test fails, use the first derivative test.
Points of diminishing returns — in applications an inflection point is often where growth stops accelerating.

example.q: Classify the critical numbers of f(x) = x³ − 3x using the second derivative test.
steps: f′(x) = 3x² − 3; critical numbers −1 and 1.
f′′(x) = 6x. At x = −1: f′′(−1) = −6 < 0 → concave down → local max, f(−1) = 2.
At x = 1: f′′(1) = 6 > 0 → concave up → local min, f(1) = −2.
f′′(0) = 0 and the sign of f′′ changes at 0, so (0, 0) is an inflection point.
example.a: Local max at (−1, 2), local min at (1, −2), inflection point at (0, 0).

practice.q: Show the second derivative test fails for f(x) = x⁴ at 0, then classify 0 another way.
practice.a: f′′(0) = 0 — inconclusive. But f(x) = x⁴ ≥ 0 = f(0), so 0 is an absolute min (the first derivative test also shows − to +).

practice.q: Find the inflection points of f(x) = x³ − 6x².
practice.a: f′′ = 6x − 12 = 0 at x = 2, with a sign change, so (2, −16) is the inflection point.

lessons.takeaway: f′′ > 0 cups up (min), f′′ < 0 cups down (max) — and when f′′(c) = 0, fall back to the sign chart.

lessons.title: Optimization Problems
lessons.intro: Optimization turns a word problem into a function of one variable and finds its extreme value. The mathematics is the extrema machinery you already know; the skill is the translation.
concepts: Recipe — draw and label; write the quantity to optimize; write the constraint; use the constraint to eliminate all but one variable; differentiate and test critical numbers and endpoints.
Domain first — the physical situation restricts the variable (lengths positive, etc.), and the optimum is often at a critical number inside that domain.
Closed vs open domains — on a closed domain also check endpoints; justify an interior optimum with the first or second derivative test.
Units and sanity — check the answer's units and magnitude against the problem before declaring victory.

example.q: A farmer has 100 ft of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen against a long barn wall (the wall forms one side, so fence is needed for only 3 sides). Maximize the area.
steps: Let x = the length of each side perpendicular to the wall; then the parallel side is 100 − 2x. Area: A(x) = x(100 − 2x) = 100x − 2x², for 0 < x < 50.
A′(x) = 100 − 4x = 0 gives x = 25. A′′ = −4 < 0, so this is a maximum.
Parallel side: 100 − 2(25) = 50 ft. Maximum area: A(25) = 25 · 50 = 1250 ft².
example.a: 25 ft (perpendicular) by 50 ft (parallel), maximum area 1250 ft².

practice.q: Find two positive numbers whose sum is 20 and whose product is maximal.
practice.a: P(x) = x(20 − x); P′ = 20 − 2x = 0 at x = 10. The numbers are 10 and 10, product 100.

practice.q: A closed box with a square base must have volume 32. Express surface area in terms of the base edge x.
practice.a: Height h = 32/x², so S(x) = 2x² + 4x·(32/x²) = 2x² + 128/x.

lessons.takeaway: Two equations — objective and constraint — then eliminate down to one variable and optimize honestly over its domain.

lessons.title: Newton's Method
lessons.intro: Newton's method finds roots by following tangent lines: from a guess, slide along the tangent to the x-axis and repeat. It converges astonishingly fast — and can fail spectacularly when misused.
concepts: The iteration — xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). Geometrically, xₙ₊₁ is where the tangent line at xₙ crosses the axis.
Quadratic convergence — near a simple root, the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.
When it fails — f′(xₙ) near 0 throws the next guess far away; poor starting guesses can cycle or diverge; multiple roots slow convergence.
Stopping rule — iterate until successive guesses agree to the precision you need.

example.q: Use Newton's method to solve x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 starting from x₀ = 2.
steps: One more step gives 2.09455, stable to 5 decimal places.
example.a: The root is approximately 2.09455 (this is the equation Newton himself used as an example).

practice.q: Derive the Newton iteration for √2 by applying it to f(x) = x² − 2.
practice.a: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − (xₙ² − 2)/(2xₙ) = (xₙ + 2/xₙ)/2 — the Babylonian method: average your guess with 2 divided by it.

practice.q: Starting from x₀ = 1, approximate the root of x³ − 2x − 5 = 0 — or explain the problem.
practice.a: f(1) = −6, f′(1) = 1, so x₁ = 1 − (−6)/1 = 7 — a wild jump far from the root near 2.09. The starting guess matters.

lessons.takeaway: Tangent-line iteration: blazingly fast near a good guess, unforgiving of a bad one. Always sanity-check the result in the original equation.

lessons.title: Antiderivatives
lessons.intro: An antiderivative of f is a function F with F′ = f: differentiation run in reverse. Because differentiating kills constants, every antiderivative comes as a family F(x) + C.
concepts: The +C — if F is one antiderivative of f, all of them are F(x) + C; geometrically, the graphs are vertical shifts of each other.
Basic reversals — ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C.
Linearity — antiderivatives respect sums and constant multiples, term by term.
Initial value problems — a condition like F(0) = 3 pins down the constant and selects one member of the family.

example.q: Find the antiderivative F of f(x) = 3x² + 4x − 5 with F(1) = 2.
steps: Reverse term by term: F(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x + C.
Check by differentiating: 3x² + 4x − 5 ✓.
Apply the condition: F(1) = 1 + 2 − 5 + C = C − 2 = 2, so C = 4.

practice.q: Find ∫ (√x + 1/x) dx.
A particle has velocity v(t) = 3t² and position s(0) = 5. Find s(t).
practice.a: s(t) = t³ + C, and s(0) = 5 gives s(t) = t³ + 5.

lessons.takeaway: Always verify an antiderivative by differentiating it — that check is free and catches every sign and constant error.

lessons.title: The Definite Integral
lessons.intro: The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums: slice the region under the curve into thin rectangles, add their areas, and let the slices shrink. It computes net signed area — and much more.
concepts: Riemann sum — partition [a, b] into n subintervals of width Δx = (b − a)/n; sum f(xᵢ*)·Δx over the slices.
Definition — ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim n→∞ Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx, when this limit exists (continuous functions always qualify).
Signed area — regions below the x-axis count negatively; the integral is area above minus area below.
Properties — integrals add over adjacent intervals, reverse sign when limits swap, and respect sums and constant multiples.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀² x dx two ways: geometrically, and state what the Riemann sum gives.
steps: Geometrically, the region under y = x from 0 to 2 is a triangle with base 2 and height 2.
The Riemann sums with right endpoints are Σ (2i/n)(2/n) = (4/n²)·n(n + 1)/2 = 2 + 2/n → 2 as n → ∞, confirming the definition agrees.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx by symmetry/geometry of signed area.
practice.a: 0 — x³ is odd: the area below the axis on [−1, 0] exactly cancels the area above it on [0, 1].

practice.q: Write ∫₁⁴ (x² + 1) dx as a limit of Riemann sums (do not evaluate).

lessons.takeaway: The integral is a limit of sums — but thanks to symmetry and geometry, you can often read simple ones off a picture.

lessons.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
lessons.intro: The Fundamental Theorem is the bridge of the whole subject: it says integration and differentiation are inverse operations. Part 1 differentiates an integral; Part 2 evaluates integrals with antiderivatives.
concepts: Part 1 — if g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt with f continuous, then g′(x) = f(x). An accumulation function's rate of change is the value being accumulated.
Part 1 with chain rule — d/dx ∫ₐ^(u(x)) f(t) dt = f(u(x)) · u′(x).
Part 2 — ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F of a continuous f. This is how definite integrals are actually computed.
Why it matters — Part 2 turns the impossible limit-of-sums definition into one substitution into an antiderivative.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₁³ x² dx.
steps: An antiderivative of x² is F(x) = x³/3.

practice.q: Find d/dx ∫₀ˣ t² dt, and d/dx ∫₀^(x²) cos t dt.
practice.a: Part 1 directly: x². With the chain rule: cos(x²) · 2x.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π sin x dx.
practice.a: Antiderivative −cos x: (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 + 1 = 2.

lessons.takeaway: Accumulate, then differentiate, and you're back where you started — that inverse relationship is the Fundamental Theorem.

lessons.title: Integration by Substitution
lessons.intro: Substitution is the chain rule read backwards. When an integrand contains a function and (a multiple of) its derivative, a change of variable u = g(x) collapses it into a basic integral.
concepts: The pattern — look for an 'inside function' u whose derivative du also appears as a factor in the integrand.
Mechanics — set u = g(x), compute du = g′(x) dx, rewrite the entire integral in u (no x may remain), integrate, then substitute back.
Definite integrals — change the limits to u-values: when x = a, u = g(a); then you never need to return to x.
Strategic choice — u should make the integral simpler; if the du factor isn't there (up to a constant), pick another u or another method.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx.
steps: Set u = x², so du = 2x dx and x dx = du/2. The x factor in the integrand is exactly what substitution needs.
Change limits: x = 0 → u = 0; x = 1 → u = 1.
The integral becomes ∫₀¹ eᵘ (du/2) = ½ [eᵘ]₀¹ = ½(e − 1).

practice.q: Find ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx.
practice.a: With u = x²: sin(x²) + C.

practice.q: Find ∫ cos x / sin x dx (the logarithmic pattern).
practice.a: With u = sin x, du = cos x dx: ∫ du/u = ln|sin x| + C. In general ∫ f′/f = ln|f| + C.

lessons.takeaway: Spot the inside function, hunt for its derivative beside it, and let u swallow both.

lessons.title: Applications of Integration (Area)
lessons.intro: The first great application: integrals compute areas — under a curve, and between two curves by integrating (top − bottom) across the interval where they cross.
concepts: Area under a curve — for f ≥ 0 on [a, b], the area is ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
Area between curves — A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx where f is the top function and g the bottom on the whole interval.
Find the crossings first — intersection x-values are the natural limits of integration; sketch to see which curve is on top.
Splitting — if top and bottom swap inside the interval, split the integral at the crossing.

example.q: Find the area between y = x and y = x².
steps: Intersections: x = x² gives x = 0 and x = 1.
On (0, 1), the line y = x is above the parabola y = x² (test x = ½: ½ > ¼).
A = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = ½ − ⅓ = ⅙.

practice.q: Find the area under y = √x from 0 to 4.
Set up (don't evaluate) the area between y = x² and y = 2x.
practice.a: They cross at x = 0 and x = 2, with 2x on top: A = ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx (= 4/3).

lessons.takeaway: Area between curves = ∫ (top − bottom). The sketch and the crossing points do the thinking; the integral does the arithmetic.

MATH101.mastery_rubric: To pass, students must demonstrate proficiency in calculating limits, derivatives, and basic integrals. A strong understanding of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and applications of derivatives (e.g., optimization) is required. Final course grade must be 70% or higher, with at least 60% on the final exam.

lessons.title: Integration by Parts
lessons.intro: Integration by parts is the product rule run in reverse: when an integrand is a product of two functions and a substitution won't work, you differentiate one factor and integrate the other, trading the original integral for (usually) an easier one.
concepts: Formula — ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, where u is the factor you differentiate and dv is the factor you integrate.
Choosing u — use LIATE (Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential): whichever factor comes first in that list is usually the best u.
Tabular method — for repeated parts with a polynomial factor, the table of derivatives and integrals organizes the work and stops when a derivative hits zero.
Repeated parts — sometimes you must apply parts twice, and the original integral can reappear and be solved for algebraically (the 'boomerang' trick).

example.q: Evaluate ∫x e^x dx.
steps: Choose u = x (algebraic, before exponential in LIATE) and dv = e^x dx.
Then du = dx and v = e^x.
Apply the formula: ∫x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫e^x dx.
The remaining integral is easy: x e^x − e^x + C.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫x sin x dx.
practice.a: −x cos x + sin x + C (check by differentiating: the derivative is x sin x).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫ln x dx.
practice.a: x ln x − x + C (take u = ln x, dv = dx).

lessons.takeaway: Pick u by LIATE, differentiate it, integrate dv, and the new integral should be simpler than the one you started with.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Integrals
lessons.intro: Integrals of powers of sine, cosine, tangent, and secant look messy until you use the Pythagorean identities to rewrite them. The trick is always the same: save one factor for the substitution and convert the rest.
concepts: Sine-cosine powers — if the sine power is odd, save one sin x and convert the rest with sin²x = 1 − cos²x; if the cosine power is odd, do the mirror image.
Both powers even — use the half-angle identities sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to lower the powers.
Tangent-secant — for ∫tan^m x sec^n x dx, if n is even save sec²x (the derivative of tan x); if m is odd save sec x tan x (the derivative of sec x).
The sec x integral — ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C, proved by multiplying top and bottom by sec x + tan x.

example.q: Evaluate ∫sin³x cos x dx.
steps: The cosine power is 1 (odd), so save cos x dx for the substitution and convert the sine power.
Let u = sin x, so du = cos x dx.
The integral becomes ∫u³ du = u⁴/4 + C.
Substitute back: sin⁴x/4 + C.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫cos³x dx.
practice.a: sin x − sin³x/3 + C (write cos³x = (1 − sin²x)cos x, then u = sin x).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫sin²x dx.
practice.a: x/2 − sin 2x/4 + C (use the half-angle identity).

lessons.takeaway: Save one factor for du, convert the rest with a Pythagorean identity, and the substitution falls out.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Substitution
lessons.intro: When an integrand contains √(a² − x²), √(a² + x²), or √(x² − a²), no ordinary substitution helps — but a trig substitution turns the square root into a single trig function, because the Pythagorean identities are built for exactly that.
concepts: The three cases — √(a² − x²) calls for x = a sin θ; √(a² + x²) calls for x = a tan θ; √(x² − a²) calls for x = a sec θ.
Why it works — each substitution makes the expression under the root a perfect square via sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, or sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ.
Returning to x — draw the right triangle for the substitution (or use θ = arcsin(x/a) etc.) to convert trig functions of θ back to expressions in x.
Definite integrals — change the limits to θ-values at the substitution step and never convert back.

example.q: Evaluate ∫dx/√(9 − x²).
steps: The form √(9 − x²) calls for x = 3 sin θ, so dx = 3 cos θ dθ.
The root becomes √(9 − 9 sin²θ) = 3√(cos²θ) = 3 cos θ (for θ in (−π/2, π/2)).
The integral becomes ∫(3 cos θ)/(3 cos θ) dθ = ∫dθ = θ + C.
Since x = 3 sin θ, θ = arcsin(x/3).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫dx/(x² + 4).
practice.a: (1/2) arctan(x/2) + C (substitute x = 2 tan θ).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫√(x² − 1)/x dx for x > 1.
practice.a: √(x² − 1) − arcsec x + C (substitute x = sec θ; the integral becomes ∫tan²θ dθ).

lessons.takeaway: Match the root to its substitution, let the Pythagorean identity collapse the root, and draw the triangle to get back to x.

lessons.title: Partial Fractions
lessons.intro: A rational function can be split into a sum of simple fractions whose denominators are the factors of the original denominator — and each simple fraction integrates to a logarithm or an arctangent. Partial fractions turns one hard integral into several easy ones.
concepts: Setup — factor the denominator completely; a linear factor (x − a) contributes A/(x − a); a repeated factor (x − a)² contributes A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²; an irreducible quadratic contributes (Ax + B)/(x² + bx + c).
Solving for the constants — clear denominators and either match coefficients or plug in strategic x-values (the roots make terms vanish).
Long division first — if the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's, divide first and decompose only the remainder.
Integration — each A/(x − a) term integrates to A ln|x − a|; quadratic terms complete the square and give arctan or a log.

example.q: Evaluate ∫dx/((x − 1)(x + 2)).
steps: Clear denominators: 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫(2x + 1)/(x(x + 1)) dx.
practice.a: ln|x(x + 1)| + C (the decomposition is 1/x + 1/(x + 1)).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫dx/(x² − 4).

lessons.takeaway: Factor, split into simple fractions, solve for the constants with strategic x-values, then integrate term by term.

lessons.title: Improper Integrals
lessons.intro: Some integrals stretch to infinity or blow up at a point inside the interval. They are not ordinary integrals at all — they are limits of ordinary integrals, and that limit may or may not exist.
concepts: Two kinds — an infinite limit of integration (∫ₐ^∞) or an integrand that is unbounded at an endpoint or interior point.
Definition — replace the problem spot by a variable bound, integrate normally, then take the limit; the integral converges only if that limit is finite.
The p-test — ∫₁^∞ dx/x^p converges exactly when p > 1, and diverges for p ≤ 1.
Comparison — if 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) and ∫g converges, then ∫f converges; if ∫f diverges, then ∫g diverges.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₁^∞ dx/x², or show it diverges.
steps: Replace ∞ by a finite bound b: ∫₁^b dx/x² = [−1/x]₁ᵇ = 1 − 1/b.
Take the limit as b → ∞: 1/b → 0.
The limit is 1, a finite number, so the integral converges.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) dx.
practice.a: 1 (the antiderivative is −e^(−x); the limit at ∞ is 0 and at 0 it is −1).

practice.q: Does ∫₀¹ dx/√x converge? If so, to what?
practice.a: Yes — it converges to 2 (the antiderivative 2√x is finite at both ends).

lessons.takeaway: An improper integral is a limit in disguise: integrate to a finite bound first, then let the bound approach the problem spot.

lessons.title: Area Between Curves
lessons.intro: The area between two curves is the integral of the vertical (or horizontal) distance between them. The only new work versus area under one curve is finding where the curves cross, so you know which one is on top and where to stop.
concepts: Setup — area = ∫ₐᵇ [top(x) − bottom(x)] dx, where a and b are the x-values where the curves intersect.
Finding intersections — solve f(x) = g(x); those solutions are the limits of integration.
Swapping roles — if the curves cross inside the interval, split the integral at the crossing; if it is easier to integrate with respect to y, use ∫[right(y) − left(y)] dy.
Signed vs. total area — (f − g) can be negative where g is on top; area is always the integral of the positive distance.

example.q: Find the area between y = x² and y = x.
steps: Intersect: x² = x gives x(x − 1) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 1.
On [0, 1], the line y = x is above the parabola y = x².
Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹.

practice.q: Find the area between y = x² and y = 2x.
practice.a: 4/3 (they cross at 0 and 2; integrate 2x − x² from 0 to 2).

practice.q: Find the area under y = sin x from 0 to π (between the curve and the x-axis).

lessons.takeaway: Intersect first, identify the top curve, and integrate the gap — never integrate a difference that changes sign.

lessons.title: Volumes by Disks/Washers
lessons.intro: Revolve a region around an axis and it sweeps out a solid. Slice that solid perpendicular to the axis and every slice is a disk (or a washer, if the region doesn't touch the axis) — integrate the cross-sectional areas and you have the volume.
concepts: Disks — revolving the area under y = f(x) about the x-axis gives V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx: each slice is a disk of radius f(x).
Washers — if the region is between an outer curve R(x) and an inner curve r(x), each slice is a washer with area π(R² − r²).
Axis choice — revolving about the y-axis usually means slicing horizontally and integrating with respect to y.
Units check — the integrand is an area (length²), integrated over a length, giving length³, as a volume should.

example.q: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region under y = √x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, about the x-axis.
steps: A slice at position x is a disk of radius √x, so its area is π(√x)² = πx.
Volume = π∫₀⁴ x dx = π[x²/2]₀⁴.
Evaluate: π(16/2 − 0) = 8π.

practice.q: Revolve the region under y = x², 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, about the x-axis. Find the volume.
practice.a: π/5 (integrate πx⁴ from 0 to 1).

practice.q: Revolve the region between y = x and y = x² about the x-axis. Find the volume.
practice.a: 2π/15 (washer: outer radius x, inner radius x², integrate π(x² − x⁴) from 0 to 1).

lessons.takeaway: Slice perpendicular to the axis, write each slice's area as πR² (or π(R² − r²)), and integrate.

lessons.title: Volumes by Cylindrical Shells
lessons.intro: Sometimes disks are the wrong tool — when the region is described nicely in x but the axis is vertical, slicing horizontally is painful. Cylindrical shells slice parallel to the axis instead, and each slice unrolls into a thin rectangle.
concepts: Shell formula — revolving about a vertical axis: V = 2π∫ (shell radius)(shell height) dx, where the radius is the distance from the slice to the axis.
When to use shells — reach for them when the axis of rotation is parallel to the slicing direction, or when solving for the inverse function would be ugly.
Radius and height — the radius is measured from the axis to the slice; the height is the top function minus the bottom function at that slice.
Mirror image — revolving about a horizontal axis gives shells in y: V = 2π∫ (radius)(height) dy.

example.q: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region under y = x², 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, about the y-axis.
steps: A shell at position x has radius x and height x² (the curve's value).
Volume = 2π∫₀² x · x² dx = 2π∫₀² x³ dx.
Integrate: 2π[x⁴/4]₀² = 2π · 4 = 8π.

practice.q: Revolve the region under y = √x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, about the y-axis. Find the volume.
practice.a: 4π/5 (integrate 2πx^(3/2) from 0 to 1).

practice.q: Revolve the region between y = x and y = x² about the y-axis. Find the volume.
practice.a: π/6 (integrate 2πx(x − x²) from 0 to 1).

lessons.takeaway: When the axis runs parallel to your slices, use shells: 2π times radius times height, integrated across the region.

lessons.title: Arc Length
lessons.intro: A curve's length is the limit of the lengths of tiny straight segments approximating it. Each segment has length √(dx² + dy²), and summing them gives an integral involving the derivative — which is why only a few arc lengths come out cleanly.
concepts: Formula — for y = f(x) on [a, b], L = ∫ₐᵇ √(1 + (f'(x))²) dx.
Why it works — a tiny segment has length √((Δx)² + (Δy)²) = √(1 + (Δy/Δx)²) Δx, and Δy/Δx → f'(x).
Nice cases — the integral is often impossible in elementary terms; the textbook cases are the ones where 1 + (f')² turns out to be a perfect square.
Parametric form — for x = x(t), y = y(t), L = ∫√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.

example.q: Find the length of y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 3.
steps: Differentiate: y' = x^(1/2), so (y')² = x.
The integrand is √(1 + x).

practice.q: Find the length of y = x³/6 + 1/(2x) from x = 1 to x = 2.
practice.a: 17/12 (here 1 + (y')² = (x²/2 + 1/(2x²))², a perfect square).

practice.q: Find the length of y = x²/2 from x = 0 to x = 1.

lessons.takeaway: Arc length is ∫√(1 + (f')²) dx — set it up, and hope the square root simplifies.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Revolution
lessons.intro: Revolve a curve around an axis and it sweeps out a surface — a cone from a line, a sphere from a semicircle. Each tiny arc of the curve traces a thin band, and adding the bands gives the surface area.
concepts: Formula — revolving y = f(x) about the x-axis: S = 2π∫ₐᵇ f(x)√(1 + (f'(x))²) dx.
Anatomy — 2πf(x) is the circumference of the band at x, and √(1 + (f')²) dx is the band's slant width (the arc-length element).
About the y-axis — use S = 2π∫ x√(1 + (f'(x))²) dx, with the radius now the x-coordinate.
Check against geometry — a line revolved about the x-axis makes a cone; a semicircle makes a sphere of area 4πr².

example.q: Find the surface area obtained by revolving y = √x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, about the x-axis.

practice.q: Revolve y = x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, about the x-axis (a cone). Find the surface area.
practice.a: π√2 (agrees with the cone formula πr·l with r = 1, l = √2).

practice.q: Revolve the semicircle y = √(1 − x²), −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, about the x-axis. Find the surface area.
practice.a: 4π — the surface area of the unit sphere.

lessons.takeaway: Surface area is circumference times slant width, integrated: 2π∫ f(x)√(1 + (f')²) dx.

lessons.title: Sequences
lessons.intro: A sequence is a list of numbers in order — a function from the natural numbers to the reals. Calculus II starts here because series are built from sequences, and the first question is always the same: do the terms settle down to a limit, or not?
concepts: Notation — a sequence is written {aₙ} or a₁, a₂, a₃, …; aₙ is the nth term.
Convergence — aₙ → L means the terms get arbitrarily close to L as n grows; formally, lim n→∞ aₙ = L.
Limit laws apply — the limit of a sequence can be computed with the same rules as limits of functions, including dividing top and bottom by the highest power of n.
Monotone convergence — a bounded, monotone sequence always converges; this is the workhorse behind many convergence proofs.
Squeeze — if aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ cₙ and the outer sequences share a limit, so does bₙ.

example.q: Find lim n→∞ (3n + 1)/(2n − 5).
steps: Divide numerator and denominator by n: (3 + 1/n)/(2 − 5/n).
As n → ∞, 1/n → 0 and 5/n → 0.
The limit is 3/2.

practice.q: Find lim n→∞ n²/(n² + 1).
practice.a: 1 (divide by n²).

practice.q: Does the sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ converge?
practice.a: No — it oscillates between −1 and 1 and never settles.

lessons.takeaway: Treat a sequence like a function of n: divide by the dominant power and read off the limit.

lessons.title: Series and Convergence
lessons.intro: A series is an infinite sum, and the question is whether adding infinitely many terms produces a finite number. The partial sums — the running totals — decide: if they approach a limit, the series converges to it.
concepts: Partial sums — S_N = a₁ + … + a_N; the series Σaₙ converges to S if S_N → S.
Geometric series — Σₙ₌₀^∞ arⁿ converges to a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1, and diverges otherwise.
Divergence test — if aₙ does not tend to 0, the series diverges; but aₙ → 0 does NOT guarantee convergence (the harmonic series is the famous counterexample).
Telescoping series — when partial sums collapse to a few surviving terms, the limit is easy to read off.
Linearity — convergent series can be added term by term and multiplied by constants.

example.q: Find the sum of Σₙ₌₀^∞ (1/2)ⁿ.
steps: This is geometric with a = 1 and r = 1/2.
Since |r| = 1/2 < 1, it converges to a/(1 − r).

practice.q: Find the sum of Σₙ₌₀^∞ (3/4)ⁿ.
practice.a: 4 (geometric with a = 1, r = 3/4).

practice.q: Does Σ n/(n + 1) converge?
practice.a: No — the terms tend to 1, not 0, so the series diverges by the divergence test.

lessons.takeaway: Convergence is about the partial sums; geometric series and the divergence test settle the easy cases.

lessons.title: Integral Test and P-Series
lessons.intro: When the terms of a series come from a positive decreasing function, the series and the improper integral of that function stand or fall together. That single idea classifies the whole family of p-series at once.
concepts: Integral test — if f is continuous, positive, and decreasing, then Σf(n) and ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx either both converge or both diverge.
Why it works — the sum is sandwiched between two Riemann sums for the integral, so finiteness of one forces finiteness of the other.
P-series — Σ1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1; the harmonic series (p = 1) diverges, slowly.
Remainder estimate — the integral test also bounds the error of a partial sum: ∫_{N+1}^∞ f ≤ R_N ≤ ∫_N^∞ f.

example.q: Does Σ 1/n² converge? Does Σ 1/√n converge?
steps: Both are p-series: Σ1/n^p with p = 2 and p = 1/2.
The p-test says Σ1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1.
p = 2 > 1, so Σ1/n² converges; p = 1/2 < 1, so Σ1/√n diverges.

practice.q: Does Σ 1/n³ converge?
practice.a: Yes — p = 3 > 1.

practice.q: Does Σ 1/(n ln n) (starting at n = 2) converge?
practice.a: No — the integral ∫₂^∞ dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x) evaluated to ∞, so the series diverges by the integral test.

lessons.takeaway: For a positive decreasing series, check the integral instead — and remember p > 1 is the whole p-series story.

lessons.title: Comparison Tests
lessons.intro: Most series are not p-series and have no integral you want to compute. Comparison tests let you judge a series by a simpler one you already understand: if your terms are smaller than a convergent series' terms, yours converges too.
concepts: Direct comparison — if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges; if Σaₙ diverges, then Σbₙ diverges.
Limit comparison — if aₙ/bₙ → L with 0 < L < ∞, then Σaₙ and Σbₙ converge or diverge together.
Choosing the comparison — ignore lower-order terms and constants: for a rational expression, compare with 1/n^(degree difference).
One direction only — direct comparison cannot prove divergence from a larger divergent series, nor convergence from a smaller divergent one.

example.q: Does Σ 1/(2ⁿ − 1) converge?
steps: Compare with the geometric series Σ1/2ⁿ, which converges.
Σ2/2ⁿ converges (geometric), so by direct comparison Σ1/(2ⁿ − 1) converges.

practice.q: Does Σ 1/(n² + n) converge?
practice.a: Yes — 1/(n² + n) < 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges.

practice.q: Does Σ (2n + 1)/(n² + 1) converge?
practice.a: No — limit comparison with 1/n gives limit 2, and the harmonic series diverges.

lessons.takeaway: Compare with the series you get by keeping only the dominant terms; the limit comparison test makes the judgment rigorous.

lessons.title: Alternating Series Test
lessons.intro: A series whose signs alternate can converge even when the absolute values add up to infinity — the positive and negative terms cancel each other out, one step at a time. The alternating harmonic series is the classic example: it converges to ln 2.
concepts: Alternating series test — if bₙ decreases to 0, then Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ converges.
Conditional vs. absolute — a series converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges; it converges conditionally if it converges but not absolutely.
Error bound — for a convergent alternating series, the error of the Nth partial sum is at most the first omitted term: |R_N| ≤ b_{N+1}.
Both conditions matter — the terms must decrease AND tend to zero; a series like Σ(−1)ⁿn/(n+1) fails the second and diverges.

example.q: Does Σₙ₌₁^∞ (−1)ⁿ/n converge? Absolutely or conditionally?
steps: The terms alternate in sign, with bₙ = 1/n decreasing to 0.
By the alternating series test, the series converges.
But Σ|(−1)ⁿ/n| = Σ1/n is the harmonic series, which diverges.
So the convergence is conditional, not absolute.

practice.q: Does Σ(−1)ⁿ/n² converge absolutely?
practice.a: Yes — Σ1/n² converges, so the series converges absolutely.

practice.q: Estimate the error in using the first 10 partial sums of Σ(−1)ⁿ/n to approximate its sum.
practice.a: At most 1/11 — the error is bounded by the first omitted term b₁₁.

lessons.takeaway: Alternating, decreasing to zero means convergence — and the next term bounds your error.

lessons.title: Ratio and Root Tests
lessons.intro: When terms involve factorials, exponentials, or nth powers, comparison tests are clumsy. The ratio and root tests judge a series by the growth rate of its own terms — how fast they shrink, relative to the previous term or to their nth root.
concepts: Ratio test — let L = lim |a_{n+1}/aₙ|. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges; if L = 1 the test is inconclusive.
Root test — let L = lim (|aₙ|)^(1/n). The same three outcomes apply; it is the natural choice when aₙ is an nth power.
When to use which — factorials and products call for the ratio test; nth powers call for the root test.
Inconclusive at L = 1 — p-series all give L = 1 under the ratio test, so a ratio of 1 sends you back to the comparison or integral tests.

example.q: Does Σ n!/nⁿ converge?
steps: Apply the ratio test: a_{n+1}/aₙ = [(n+1)!/(n+1)^(n+1)] · [nⁿ/n!].
Simplify: (n+1)!/n! = n+1, so the ratio is (n+1)nⁿ/(n+1)^(n+1) = nⁿ/(n+1)ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ.
As n → ∞, (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e, so the ratio tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368 < 1.
By the ratio test, the series converges.

practice.q: Does Σ 2ⁿ/n! converge?
practice.a: Yes — the ratio test gives limit 0.

practice.q: Does Σ nⁿ/3ⁿ converge?
practice.a: No — the root test gives (nⁿ/3ⁿ)^(1/n) = n/3 → ∞, so it diverges.

lessons.takeaway: Factorials → ratio test, nth powers → root test, and L = 1 means 'try something else'.

lessons.title: Power Series
lessons.intro: A power series is a polynomial that never ends: Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ. It converges on an interval around its center and diverges outside it — and inside that interval, it behaves like a function you can differentiate and integrate term by term.
concepts: Radius of convergence — there is a number R (possibly 0 or ∞) such that the series converges absolutely for |x − a| < R and diverges for |x − a| > R.
Finding R — apply the ratio or root test to the general term; the resulting inequality in |x − a| reveals R.
Endpoints — the ratio test says nothing at |x − a| = R, so test each endpoint separately with the series tests.
Term-by-term calculus — inside the interval of convergence, you may differentiate and integrate a power series term by term; the radius stays the same.

example.q: Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n!.
steps: Apply the ratio test: |a_{n+1}/aₙ| = |x|^(n+1)/(n+1)! · n!/|x|ⁿ = |x|/(n+1).
As n → ∞, this tends to 0 for every x.
So the series converges for all x: radius R = ∞, interval (−∞, ∞).

practice.q: Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n.
practice.a: R = 1, interval [−1, 1): at x = 1 the harmonic series diverges; at x = −1 the alternating harmonic series converges.

practice.q: Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ (x − 2)ⁿ/n².
practice.a: R = 1, interval [1, 3]: both endpoints give convergent p-series (Σ1/n² and Σ(−1)ⁿ/n²).

lessons.takeaway: The ratio test gives the radius; the endpoints always need their own separate check.

lessons.title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series
lessons.intro: A Taylor series represents a function as a power series built from its derivatives at a single point. It is how calculators compute sin, cos, and e^x — and how we approximate complicated functions with polynomials.
concepts: Formula — f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! · (x − a)ⁿ, when the series converges to f; a = 0 gives a Maclaurin series.
Famous Maclaurin series — e^x = Σxⁿ/n!; sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − ⋯; cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − ⋯; 1/(1 − x) = Σxⁿ for |x| < 1.
Building new series — differentiate, integrate, substitute, or multiply known series instead of computing derivatives from scratch.
Taylor polynomials and error — the Nth Taylor polynomial approximates f near a; Taylor's inequality bounds the error with the next derivative.

example.q: Write the Maclaurin series for e^x and use it to approximate e^0.1 to four decimal places.
steps: All derivatives of e^x are e^x, and e^0 = 1, so the Maclaurin series is Σxⁿ/n! = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ⋯.
The true value e^0.1 ≈ 1.1051702, so four terms already give four correct decimal places.

practice.q: Write the Maclaurin series for sin x and approximate sin(0.2).
Use the geometric series to find the Maclaurin series for ln(1 + x).
practice.a: ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − x⁴/4 + ⋯ (integrate 1/(1 + x) = Σ(−x)ⁿ term by term).

lessons.takeaway: Know the four famous Maclaurin series by heart — every other Taylor series is built from them.

lessons.title: Parametric Curves
lessons.intro: Some curves are easier to describe by a third variable — a parameter — than by an equation in x and y. A circle traced by time, a projectile's path, a cycloid rolled by a wheel: parametric equations x = f(t), y = g(t) capture motion, not just shape.
concepts: Definition — a parametric curve is the set of points (f(t), g(t)) as t ranges over an interval; t is the parameter, often time.
Eliminating the parameter — solve one equation for t and substitute into the other to get a Cartesian equation (when possible).
Slope — dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0; the parameter's derivatives give the tangent slope directly.
Vertical tangents — when dx/dt = 0 but dy/dt ≠ 0, the curve has a vertical tangent at that point.

example.q: For x = t², y = t³, find dy/dx and the tangent slope at t = 2.
steps: Differentiate with respect to t: dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 3t².
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2.
At t = 2, the point is (4, 8) and the slope is 3(2)/2 = 3.
example.a: dy/dx = 3t/2; at t = 2 the slope is 3

practice.q: Eliminate the parameter for x = cos t, y = sin t. What curve is it?
practice.a: x² + y² = 1 — the unit circle.

practice.q: For x = t² − 1, y = 2t, find dy/dx in terms of t.
practice.a: dy/dx = 1/t (dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2).

lessons.takeaway: Parametrize by t, eliminate when you need Cartesian form, and divide the t-derivatives for the slope.

lessons.title: Calculus with Parametric Curves
lessons.intro: Once a curve is parametric, the calculus follows the parameter: arc length integrates the speed √( (dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² ), and area under the curve integrates y dx/dt. The formulas are the familiar ones, rewritten in t.
concepts: Arc length — L = ∫_α^β √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt; the integrand is the speed of the point moving along the curve.
Area — the area under a parametric curve (traced left to right) is ∫_α^β y(t) · x'(t) dt.
Second derivative — d²y/dx² = (d/dt)(dy/dx) / (dx/dt); use it to find concavity and inflection points.
Speed vs. length — the speed at an instant is the integrand of the arc-length formula; length is its integral over time.

example.q: Find the length of one arch of the cycloid x = t − sin t, y = 1 − cos t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.
steps: dx/dt = 1 − cos t and dy/dt = sin t.
Speed = √((1 − cos t)² + sin²t) = √(2 − 2 cos t) = 2|sin(t/2)|; on [0, 2π] this is 2 sin(t/2).

practice.q: Find the length of x = t², y = 2t from t = 0 to t = 1.
practice.a: √2 + ln(1 + √2) (the integral is 2∫₀¹√(t² + 1) dt).

practice.q: Find the area under the parametric curve x = t, y = t² from t = 0 to t = 2.
practice.a: 8/3 (integrate y·x'(t) = t² from 0 to 2).

lessons.takeaway: In t, arc length integrates the speed and area integrates y times dx/dt.

lessons.title: Polar Coordinates
lessons.intro: Polar coordinates locate a point by how far it is from the origin and in which direction — (r, θ) instead of (x, y). Curves with circular or rotational symmetry, like cardioids and spirals, become simple in polar form.
concepts: Conversion — x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ; r² = x² + y² and tan θ = y/x.
Non-uniqueness — the same point has many polar names: (r, θ) = (r, θ + 2π) = (−r, θ + π).
Polar equations — r = a is a circle of radius |a| centered at the origin; θ = c is a line through the origin; r = a cos θ and r = a sin θ are circles through the origin.
Graphing — plot by sampling θ, computing r, and remembering that a negative r means 'plot in the opposite direction'.

example.q: Convert r = 2 cos θ to a Cartesian equation and identify the curve.
steps: Multiply both sides by r: r² = 2r cos θ.
Replace r² by x² + y² and r cos θ by x: x² + y² = 2x.
Complete the square: (x − 1)² + y² = 1.
This is a circle of radius 1 centered at (1, 0).

practice.q: Convert the polar point (2, π/3) to rectangular coordinates.
Convert the rectangular point (1, 1) to polar coordinates (r > 0, 0 ≤ θ < 2π).

lessons.takeaway: Polar form trades (x, y) for (distance, direction) — and circles through the origin become one-term equations.

lessons.title: Area and Arc Length in Polar Coordinates
lessons.intro: In polar coordinates, area is built from tiny sectors, not rectangles: a sector of angle dθ and radius r has area (1/2)r² dθ. Arc length follows the same idea as parametric curves, with the radius playing the role of the moving point.
concepts: Area — the area swept by r = f(θ) from θ = a to θ = b is A = (1/2)∫ₐᵇ [f(θ)]² dθ.
Why (1/2)r² — a circular sector of radius r and angle dθ has area (1/2)r² dθ; integrating sweeps the region.
Arc length — L = ∫ₐᵇ √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ.
Watch the range — trace the curve once: a full cardioid needs θ from 0 to 2π, but a circle r = sin θ is traced completely by 0 to π (r goes negative after that and retraces).

example.q: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.
steps: Area = (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (1 + cos θ)² dθ.
Expand: (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (1 + 2 cos θ + cos²θ) dθ.
Integrate term by term: ∫₀^{2π} 1 dθ = 2π, ∫₀^{2π} 2 cos θ dθ = 0, ∫₀^{2π} cos²θ dθ = π.

practice.q: Find the area enclosed by the circle r = 2.
practice.a: 4π (the formula gives (1/2)∫₀^{2π} 4 dθ = 4π, matching πr²).

practice.q: Find the arc length of the cardioid r = 1 + sin θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
practice.a: 8 (the integrand simplifies to √(2 + 2 sin θ) = 2|sin(θ/2 + π/4)|, whose integral over a full period is 8).

lessons.takeaway: Polar area integrates (1/2)r² dθ; polar arc length integrates √(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ.

MATH102.mastery_rubric: To pass, students must master various integration techniques and their applications, especially in calculating volumes and arc lengths. A solid grasp of convergence tests for sequences and series, and the ability to work with power, Taylor, and Maclaurin series, is essential. Final course grade must be 70% or higher, with at least 60% on the final exam.

modules.module_title: Vectors and the Geometry of Space

lessons.title: 3D Coordinate Systems
lessons.intro: Calculus in three dimensions starts with a place to stand: the xyz-coordinate system adds a z-axis perpendicular to the familiar xy-plane, so every point is an ordered triple (x, y, z) and every geometric idea from 2D — distance, midpoints, circles — gains one more coordinate.
concepts: Octants — the three coordinate planes (x = 0, y = 0, z = 0) divide space into eight octants; the first octant has x, y, z all positive.
Distance formula — the distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is √((x2−x1)² + (y2−y1)² + (z2−z1)²), the Pythagorean theorem applied twice.
Midpoint — average each coordinate: the midpoint of P and Q is ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2, (z1+z2)/2).
Spheres — the sphere with center (h, k, l) and radius r is (x−h)² + (y−k)² + (z−l)² = r²; completing the square recovers a center and radius from a general equation.

example.q: Find the distance between P(1, 2, 3) and Q(4, 6, 3), and the midpoint of PQ.
steps: So the distance is 5.

practice.q: Find the distance from the origin to (3, 4, 12).
Write the equation of the sphere with center (1, −2, 3) and radius 4.

lessons.takeaway: Every 2D distance idea carries over with one extra coordinate: square the difference in each coordinate, add, and take the square root.

lessons.title: Vectors
lessons.intro: A vector is a quantity with magnitude and direction — displacement, velocity, force. In coordinates it is an ordered triple ⟨a, b, c⟩, and vectors add component-wise and scale by multiplying every component.
concepts: Magnitude — |⟨a, b, c⟩| = √(a² + b² + c²); a vector with magnitude 1 is a unit vector.
Addition and scaling — ⟨a, b, c⟩ + ⟨d, e, f⟩ = ⟨a+d, b+e, c+f⟩ and k⟨a, b, c⟩ = ⟨ka, kb, kc⟩; geometrically, addition is the parallelogram (or tip-to-tail) rule.
Unit vector — the unit vector in the direction of v is v/|v|.
Position vs. displacement — the vector from P(x1, y1, z1) to Q(x2, y2, z2) is ⟨x2−x1, y2−y1, z2−z1⟩.

example.q: Let a = ⟨2, −1, 3⟩ and b = ⟨1, 0, −2⟩. Find a + b, 2a − b, and |a|.

practice.q: Find the unit vector in the direction of ⟨1, 2, 2⟩.
practice.a: ⟨1/3, 2/3, 2/3⟩ (the magnitude is 3).

lessons.takeaway: Vectors add and scale component by component; divide by the magnitude to get a unit vector in the same direction.

lessons.title: Dot Product
lessons.intro: The dot product turns two vectors into a single number that measures how much they point in the same direction. It is the key to angles, projections, and the physics idea of work.
concepts: Component formula — a · b = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3.
Geometric formula — a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors (0 ≤ θ ≤ π).
Orthogonality — a · b = 0 (for nonzero vectors) exactly when the vectors are perpendicular.
Projection — the scalar projection of b onto a is (a · b)/|a|, and the vector projection is ((a · b)/|a|²) a.

example.q: Let a = ⟨2, 3, −1⟩ and b = ⟨1, −2, 4⟩. Find a · b and the angle between them.
steps: θ = arccos(−0.467) ≈ 117.8°. The negative dot product means the angle is obtuse.

practice.q: Find the angle between a = ⟨1, −1, 2⟩ and b = ⟨3, 0, −1⟩.
A force F = ⟨5, 2, 0⟩ N moves an object along d = ⟨3, 4, 0⟩ m. Find the work done.

lessons.takeaway: Dot product zero means perpendicular; its sign tells you whether the angle is acute or obtuse.

lessons.title: Cross Product
lessons.intro: The cross product of two vectors is a new vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span. It is how we build normals to planes and measure torque.
concepts: Component formula — a × b = ⟨a2b3 − a3b2, a3b1 − a1b3, a1b2 − a2b1⟩, computed with a 3×3 determinant whose first row is i, j, k.
Magnitude — |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b; half of it is the area of the triangle.
Direction — the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand from a to b and your thumb points along a × b.
Algebra — a × b = −(b × a); a × a = 0; a × b = 0 exactly when a and b are parallel.

example.q: Let a = ⟨1, 2, 3⟩ and b = ⟨4, 5, 6⟩. Find a × b and the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b.
steps: That magnitude is the parallelogram's area.

practice.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 3).
practice.a: √46/2 (the cross product of the side vectors is ⟨6, −3, 1⟩, magnitude √46, halved).

lessons.takeaway: Cross product: determinant for the components, magnitude for the parallelogram area, right-hand rule for the direction.

lessons.title: Equations of Lines and Planes
lessons.intro: A line in 3D is pinned down by a point and a direction vector; a plane by a point and a normal vector. Both come from the dot and cross products of the previous lessons.
concepts: Vector equation of a line — r = r0 + t v, where r0 is a position vector of a point on the line and v is a direction vector; t ranges over all reals.
Symmetric equations — (x−x0)/a = (y−y0)/b = (z−z0)/c for direction ⟨a, b, c⟩ (omit a fraction if its denominator is 0).
Equation of a plane — n · (r − r0) = 0, i.e. a(x−x0) + b(y−y0) + c(z−z0) = 0 for normal n = ⟨a, b, c⟩.
Distances — the distance from a point to the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is |ax0 + by0 + cz0 + d|/√(a² + b² + c²).

example.q: Find an equation of the plane through (1, 0, −2) with normal ⟨3, −1, 2⟩, and the distance from (2, 1, 0) to the plane x + 2y − 2z = 5.
steps: So the distance is 1/3.

practice.q: Find symmetric equations for the line through (0, 1, 1) and (2, 3, −1).
Find an equation of the plane through (1, 1, 1), (1, 2, 0), and (2, 0, 1).
practice.a: x + y + z = 3 (a normal is ⟨−1, −1, −1⟩ from the cross product of the edge vectors).

lessons.takeaway: Line: point plus direction vector. Plane: point plus normal vector — and the cross product builds a normal from two vectors in the plane.

lessons.title: Cylinders and Quadric Surfaces
lessons.intro: Quadric surfaces are the 3D analogues of conic sections: the graphs of second-degree equations in x, y, z. Their traces — slices by coordinate planes — reveal which of the six classic shapes you are looking at.
concepts: Cylinders — an equation missing one variable, e.g. x² + y² = 4, is a cylinder: the 2D curve extruded along the missing axis.
Ellipsoid — x²/a² + y²/b² + z²/c² = 1, a stretched sphere with all traces ellipses.
Paraboloid — z = x²/a² + y²/b² (elliptic) or z = x²/a² − y²/b² (hyperbolic saddle): traces are parabolas and ellipses or hyperbolas.
Hyperboloids and cones — x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 1 is a hyperboloid of one sheet; with −1 it is two sheets; x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 0 is a cone.

example.q: Identify the surface x² + y² − z² = 1 and describe its traces in the planes z = 0 and y = 0.
steps: Two positive squares and one negative square, equal to 1: a hyperboloid of one sheet.
At z = 0 the trace is x² + y² = 1, a circle of radius 1 (the 'waist').
At y = 0 the trace is x² − z² = 1, a hyperbola opening along the x-axis.
example.a: Hyperboloid of one sheet; z = 0 trace is the unit circle, y = 0 trace is the hyperbola x² − z² = 1

practice.q: Identify the surface y = x².
practice.a: A parabolic cylinder, extruded along the z-axis.

practice.q: Identify x²/9 − y²/4 + z²/25 = 1.
practice.a: Hyperboloid of one sheet (two positive terms, one negative).

lessons.takeaway: Count the signs: all positive is an ellipsoid, one negative is a hyperboloid of one sheet, and a missing variable means a cylinder.

lessons.title: Vector Functions and Space Curves
lessons.intro: A vector function r(t) = ⟨f(t), g(t), h(t)⟩ traces a curve through space as t varies — the position of a moving particle at each instant. Each component is an ordinary function of one variable.
concepts: Parametrization — a space curve is the set of points r(t) as t runs over an interval; different parametrizations can trace the same curve.
Helix — r(t) = ⟨a cos t, a sin t, bt⟩ winds around a cylinder of radius a, rising bt per radian.
Domain — the domain of r is the intersection of the domains of its component functions.
Limits and continuity — r(t) has a limit (is continuous) exactly when each component does.

example.q: Describe the curve r(t) = ⟨2 cos t, 2 sin t, 3t⟩ and find the point where t = π/2.
steps: x² + y² = 4 cos²t + 4 sin²t = 4, so the curve lies on the cylinder of radius 2 about the z-axis.
z = 3t grows linearly, so the curve is a helix rising 3 units per radian.
example.a: A helix of radius 2 rising along the z-axis; at t = π/2 the point is (0, 2, 3π/2)

practice.q: Find the domain of r(t) = ⟨t², eᵗ, ln t⟩.
practice.a: t > 0 (ln t needs t > 0; the other components are defined everywhere).

practice.q: Find r(1) for r(t) = ⟨t², eᵗ, ln t⟩.

lessons.takeaway: Read a vector function component by component: the first two often draw a familiar plane curve while the third lifts it into space.

lessons.title: Derivatives and Integrals of Vector Functions
lessons.intro: Differentiate a vector function component by component and you get the velocity vector — tangent to the curve, pointing in the direction of motion. Integrate component by component and you recover position from velocity.
concepts: Derivative — r′(t) = ⟨f′(t), g′(t), h′(t)⟩; it is tangent to the curve at r(t).
Rules — sums, scalar multiples, and the dot- and cross-product rules all carry over from single-variable calculus.
Integral — ∫r(t) dt = ⟨∫f, ∫g, ∫h⟩ dt; a definite integral gives a displacement vector.
Unit tangent — T(t) = r′(t)/|r′(t)| is the unit vector in the direction of motion.

example.q: Let r(t) = ⟨t², sin t, eᵗ⟩. Find r′(t), r′(π/2), and ∫₀¹ ⟨t, t², 1⟩ dt.
steps: r′(t) = ⟨2t, cos t, eᵗ⟩.
example.a: r′(t) = ⟨2t, cos t, eᵗ⟩; r′(π/2) = ⟨π, 0, e^{π/2}⟩; the integral is ⟨1/2, 1/3, 1⟩

practice.q: Find r′(t) for r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t, t²⟩.
practice.a: ⟨−sin t, cos t, 2t⟩.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀² ⟨1, t, t²⟩ dt.

lessons.takeaway: Vector calculus is single-variable calculus done three times at once — once per component.

lessons.title: Arc Length and Curvature
lessons.intro: Arc length measures how far a particle travels along a curve, and curvature measures how sharply the curve bends. A circle bends at a constant rate; a straight line does not bend at all.
concepts: Arc length — from a to b the length is ∫ₐᵇ |r′(t)| dt; reparametrizing by arc length s makes |r′(s)| = 1.
Curvature — κ = |T′(t)|/|r′(t)| = |r′(t) × r″(t)|/|r′(t)|³, where T is the unit tangent.
Circle — a circle of radius a has constant curvature κ = 1/a: small circles bend sharply, large ones gently.
Plane curves — for y = f(x), κ = |f″(x)|/(1 + f′(x)²)^{3/2}.

example.q: Find the arc length of r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t, t⟩ from t = 0 to t = 2π, and the curvature of the helix.
steps: r′(t) = ⟨−sin t, cos t, 1⟩, so |r′(t)| = √(sin²t + cos²t + 1) = √2.
Length = ∫₀^{2π} √2 dt = 2π√2.
r″(t) = ⟨−cos t, −sin t, 0⟩ and r′ × r″ = ⟨sin t, −cos t, 1⟩, with |r′ × r″| = √2 and |r′|³ = 2√2, so κ = 1/2.

practice.q: Find the curvature of the circle r(t) = ⟨3 cos t, 3 sin t, 0⟩.
practice.a: κ = 1/3 (a circle of radius 3).

practice.q: Find the arc length of r(t) = ⟨t, t², 0⟩ from t = 0 to t = 1.

lessons.takeaway: Arc length integrates speed; curvature is the rate at which the unit tangent turns, per unit of arc length.

lessons.title: Motion in Space
lessons.intro: Position, velocity, and acceleration are all vectors: velocity is the derivative of position, acceleration the derivative of velocity. Splitting acceleration into tangential and normal parts separates speeding up from turning.
concepts: Velocity and speed — v(t) = r′(t); speed is |v(t)|; acceleration is a(t) = v′(t) = r″(t).
Tangential component — a_T = (v · a)/|v| measures the rate of change of speed.
Normal component — a_N = |v × a|/|v| measures turning; a_N = κ|v|², and a = a_T T + a_N N.
Projectile motion — with gravity, r(t) = ⟨v0x t, v0y t − (g/2)t², 0⟩: constant horizontal velocity, vertical acceleration −g.

example.q: A particle has position r(t) = ⟨t², t, 2t⟩. Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2, its speed then, and a_T and a_N at t = 2.

practice.q: For r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t, 0⟩, find speed, |a|, a_T, and a_N.
practice.a: Speed 1, |a| = 1, a_T = 0 (constant speed), a_N = 1 (pure turning).

practice.q: A projectile is launched with r(t) = ⟨10t, 20t − 4.9t², 0⟩. What is its velocity at t = 2?
practice.a: ⟨10, 0.4, 0⟩ (v = ⟨10, 20 − 9.8t, 0⟩, and at t = 2 the vertical component is 0.4).

lessons.takeaway: a_T tells you how fast the speed is changing; a_N tells you how fast the direction is changing.

lessons.title: Functions of Several Variables
lessons.intro: A function of two variables assigns a number to every point (x, y) in its domain — think of temperature across a map, or height above a landscape. Its graph is a surface, and its level curves are the contour lines on a topographic map.
concepts: Domain and range — the domain is the set of (x, y) where the formula makes sense; the range is the set of output values.
Graph — the graph of z = f(x, y) is the surface of points (x, y, f(x, y)) in 3D space.
Level curves — the curve f(x, y) = k is the set of points where the function has the constant value k; close-together level curves mean steep terrain.
Traces — fixing x or y slices the surface into a curve in a vertical plane.

example.q: Find the domain and range of f(x, y) = √(9 − x² − y²) and describe its level curves.
steps: The square root needs 9 − x² − y² ≥ 0, so the domain is the disk x² + y² ≤ 9.
On that disk, f ranges from 0 (at the rim) to 3 (at the origin): range [0, 3].
Level curves √(9 − x² − y²) = k are circles x² + y² = 9 − k².
The graph is the upper hemisphere of radius 3.
example.a: Domain: the disk x² + y² ≤ 9; range [0, 3]; level curves are concentric circles; graph is the upper hemisphere of radius 3

practice.q: Find the domain of f(x, y) = ln(x + y).
practice.a: x + y > 0 (the half-plane above the line y = −x).

practice.q: Evaluate f(2, 1) for f(x, y) = x² − 3xy + y².

lessons.takeaway: Domain first, then picture the surface through its level curves — the contour map of the function.

lessons.title: Limits and Continuity
