lessons.intro: For a limit in two variables to exist, the function must approach the same value along every path into the point. One bad path is enough to kill a limit — and that is what makes multivariable limits harder than single-variable ones.
concepts: Two-path test — if f approaches different values along two paths into (a, b), the limit does not exist.
Squeeze — if |f(x, y)| ≤ g(x, y) and g → 0, then f → 0; the bound |x²y/(x² + y²)| ≤ |y| is a classic.
Continuity — f is continuous at (a, b) when the limit equals f(a, b); polynomials, exponentials, and quotients (where the denominator is nonzero) are continuous.
Polar coordinates — writing x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ often reduces a limit at the origin to a statement about r → 0.

example.q: Show that lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} (x²y)/(x² + y²) = 0, and that lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} xy/(x² + y²) does not exist.
steps: For the first: |x²y/(x² + y²)| = |y| · x²/(x² + y²) ≤ |y| → 0, so by the squeeze theorem the limit is 0.
For the second, approach along y = mx: xy/(x² + y²) = mx²/(x² + m²x²) = m/(1 + m²), which depends on m.
Along y = 0 the value is 0; along y = x it is 1/2. Two paths, two values — the limit does not exist.
example.a: First limit is 0 (squeeze); second limit does not exist (path-dependent)

practice.q: Does lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} x²/(x² + y²) exist?
practice.a: No: along y = 0 it is 1, along x = 0 it is 0.

practice.q: Does lim_{(x,y)→(0,0)} (x² − y²)/(x² + y²) exist?
practice.a: No: along y = 0 it is 1, along x = 0 it is −1.

lessons.takeaway: One path is never enough to prove a limit exists; one path is enough to prove it does not.

lessons.title: Partial Derivatives
lessons.intro: A partial derivative measures the rate of change in one direction while all other variables are frozen — the slope of the surface along a line parallel to an axis. Treat the other variables as constants and differentiate as usual.
concepts: Definition — f_x(a, b) is the derivative of the single-variable function x ↦ f(x, b); f_y freezes x instead.
Notation — f_x, ∂f/∂x, D_x f all mean the same thing; second partials are f_xx, f_yy, f_xy, f_yx.
Clairaut's theorem — if the mixed partials f_xy and f_yx are continuous, they are equal.
Interpretation — f_x is the slope in the x-direction, f_y the slope in the y-direction; together they will build the tangent plane.

example.q: Let f(x, y) = x²y + y³. Find f_x, f_y, f_xx, f_yy, and f_xy.
steps: Freeze y and differentiate in x: f_x = 2xy.
Freeze x and differentiate in y: f_y = x² + 3y².
Differentiate again: f_xx = 2y and f_yy = 6y.
Mixed: f_xy = ∂/∂y (2xy) = 2x (and f_yx = ∂/∂x (x² + 3y²) = 2x, confirming Clairaut).
example.a: f_x = 2xy, f_y = x² + 3y², f_xx = 2y, f_yy = 6y, f_xy = 2x

practice.q: For f(x, y) = x³y² + sin(xy), find f_x(1, 0) and f_y(1, 0).
practice.a: f_x = 3x²y² + y cos(xy), so f_x(1, 0) = 0; f_y = 2x³y + x cos(xy), so f_y(1, 0) = 1.

practice.q: For f(x, y) = xy², find f_x, f_y, and f_xy.
practice.a: f_x = y², f_y = 2xy, f_xy = 2y.

lessons.takeaway: Partial derivatives are ordinary derivatives with the other variables held constant — and the mixed partials agree when they are continuous.

lessons.title: Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations
lessons.intro: A smooth surface is nearly flat up close: the tangent plane at a point is the best flat approximation, built from the two partial derivatives. Its formula is the multivariable version of the tangent line, and it powers linear approximation.
concepts: Tangent plane — at (a, b) with z0 = f(a, b): z = z0 + f_x(a, b)(x − a) + f_y(a, b)(y − b).
Linear approximation — L(x, y) = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x − a) + f_y(a, b)(y − b) estimates f near (a, b).
Differentials — dz = f_x dx + f_y dy estimates the change in f from small changes dx, dy.
Error — the approximation is good when (x, y) is close to (a, b); the error shrinks faster than the distance.

example.q: Find the tangent plane to z = x² + y² at (1, 2) and use it to estimate f(1.1, 1.9).
steps: Tangent plane: z = 5 + 2(x − 1) + 4(y − 2) = 2x + 4y − 5.
The true value is 1.21 + 3.61 = 4.82, so the estimate is off by only 0.02.

practice.q: Find the tangent plane to z = xy at (2, 3) and estimate f(2.1, 2.9).
practice.a: z = 6 + 3(x − 2) + 2(y − 3) = 3x + 2y − 6; estimate 6.1 (true value 6.09).

practice.q: For f(x, y) = √(x² + y²) at (3, 4), give the linear approximation and estimate f(3.1, 3.9).

lessons.takeaway: The tangent plane is the linear part of the function near a point — two partial derivatives are all it takes.

lessons.title: The Chain Rule
lessons.intro: When the inputs of a multivariable function themselves depend on t (or on more variables), the chain rule tracks how the change flows through: multiply the rate along each path and add them up.
concepts: One-parameter chain rule — if z = f(x, y) with x = x(t), y = y(t): dz/dt = f_x · dx/dt + f_y · dy/dt.
Tree diagrams — draw a branch for each intermediate variable; each path contributes a product of derivatives along it.
Several independent variables — if x and y depend on s and t, then ∂z/∂s = f_x x_s + f_y y_s (and similarly for t).
Implicit differentiation — for F(x, y) = 0, dy/dx = −F_x/F_y.

example.q: Let z = x²y with x = t² and y = t³. Find dz/dt two ways.
steps: Chain rule: dz/dt = (2xy)(2t) + (x²)(3t²).
Substitute x = t², y = t³: 2xy = 2t⁵, so the first term is 4t⁶; x² = t⁴, so the second term is 3t⁶.
dz/dt = 7t⁶.
Check by substitution: z = t⁴ · t³ = t⁷, so dz/dt = 7t⁶. ✓

practice.q: Let z = e^{xy} with x = 2t and y = t². Find dz/dt.
practice.a: dz/dt = y e^{xy} · 2 + x e^{xy} · 2t = 6t² e^{2t³}.

practice.q: Let z = ln(x + y) with x = t and y = t². Find dz/dt.
practice.a: dz/dt = (1 + 2t)/(t + t²).

lessons.takeaway: Chain rule: sum over every path from the output back to the independent variable, multiplying derivatives along each path.

lessons.title: Directional Derivatives and the Gradient Vector
lessons.intro: Partial derivatives give slopes along the axes, but a surface has a slope in every direction. The gradient vector packages both partials into one arrow that points uphill — and its dot product with a unit direction gives the slope in that direction.
concepts: Directional derivative — D_u f(a, b) = ∇f(a, b) · u, the rate of change in the direction of the unit vector u.
Gradient — ∇f = ⟨f_x, f_y⟩ (and ⟨f_x, f_y, f_z⟩ for three variables).
Steepest ascent — f increases fastest in the direction of ∇f, at the rate |∇f|; it decreases fastest in the direction −∇f.
Level curves — ∇f is perpendicular to the level curve f = k at every point.

example.q: Let f(x, y) = x² + y². At (1, 2), find the directional derivative in the direction u = ⟨3/5, 4/5⟩ and the direction and rate of steepest increase.
steps: Steepest increase is in the direction of ∇f, i.e. ⟨1, 2⟩/√5, at rate |∇f| = √20 = 2√5.
example.a: Directional derivative 22/5; steepest increase in direction ⟨1, 2⟩/√5 at rate 2√5

practice.q: For f(x, y) = xy at (2, 1), find D_u f with u = ⟨1/√2, 1/√2⟩.
For f(x, y) = xy at (2, 1), what is the maximum rate of increase?
practice.a: √5, in the direction ⟨1, 2⟩/√5.

lessons.takeaway: The gradient points uphill; dot it with a unit vector to get the slope in any direction.

lessons.title: Maximum and Minimum Values
lessons.intro: Finding the highest and lowest points of a surface means solving f_x = 0 and f_y = 0 for critical points, then using the second-derivative test to sort them into maxima, minima, and saddles — plus Lagrange multipliers when the point must lie on a curve.
concepts: Critical points — points where f_x = f_y = 0 or where a partial derivative fails to exist.
Second-derivative test — with D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)²: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 means a local min; D > 0 and f_xx < 0 means a local max; D < 0 means a saddle point.
Absolute extrema — on a closed, bounded region, check interior critical points and the boundary (often by parametrizing it).
Lagrange multipliers — to optimize f subject to g = k, solve ∇f = λ∇g together with g = k.

example.q: Find and classify the critical points of f(x, y) = x³ + y³ − 3xy.
steps: f_x = 3x² − 3y = 0 gives y = x²; f_y = 3y² − 3x = 0 gives x = y². Together: x = x⁴, so x = 0 or x = 1.
Critical points: (0, 0) and (1, 1).
D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy² = (6x)(6y) − (−3)² = 36xy − 9.
At (1, 1): D = 27 > 0 and f_xx = 6 > 0, so a local minimum with f(1, 1) = −1. At (0, 0): D = −9 < 0, so a saddle point.
example.a: Local minimum −1 at (1, 1); saddle point at (0, 0)

practice.q: Find and classify the critical point of f(x, y) = x² − 2x + y² − 6y + 10.
practice.a: Critical point (1, 3); D = 4 > 0 and f_xx = 2 > 0, so a local (in fact global) minimum with value 0.

practice.q: Use Lagrange multipliers to maximize f(x, y) = xy subject to x² + y² = 1.

lessons.takeaway: Set both partials to zero, then let D decide: positive D means an extremum (sign of f_xx tells which), negative D means a saddle.

lessons.title: Double Integrals over Rectangles
lessons.intro: A double integral over a rectangle is an iterated integral: integrate in one variable while treating the other as a constant, then integrate the result. When the integrand is continuous, Fubini's theorem says the order does not matter.
concepts: Iterated integral — ∬_R f(x, y) dA = ∫ₐᵇ ∫_c^d f(x, y) dy dx = ∫_c^d ∫ₐᵇ f(x, y) dx dy for R = [a, b] × [c, d].
Volume interpretation — if f ≥ 0, the double integral is the volume under the surface z = f(x, y) over R.
Fubini's theorem — for continuous f, both orders of integration give the same value.
Separable integrands — if f(x, y) = g(x)h(y), the double integral factors as (∫g)(∫h).

example.q: Evaluate ∬_R (3x + 2y) dA where R = [0, 1] × [0, 2].
steps: Inner integral (in y): ∫₀² (3x + 2y) dy = [3xy + y²]₀² = 6x + 4.
Outer integral: ∫₀¹ (6x + 4) dx = [3x² + 4x]₀¹ = 3 + 4 = 7.
Fubini says integrating in x first would give the same 7.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀² (x + y) dy dx.
practice.a: 3 (inner integral 2x + 2, then ∫₀¹ (2x + 2) dx = 1 + 2).

practice.q: Evaluate ∬_R x²y dA where R = [0, 2] × [0, 1].

lessons.takeaway: Integrate one variable at a time, treating the other as a constant; Fubini guarantees the order is free.

lessons.title: Iterated Integrals
lessons.intro: An iterated integral is a double integral with its limits built in — the inner limits may depend on the outer variable, which is how a region's shape gets encoded into the integral. Choosing the order that matches the region's description is half the battle.
concepts: Type I regions — between two curves y = g1(x) and y = g2(x) for a ≤ x ≤ b: integrate y first, then x.
Type II regions — between two curves x = h1(y) and x = h2(y) for c ≤ y ≤ d: integrate x first, then y.
Changing order — sketch the region, find its boundary curves, and rewrite the limits; the integrand stays the same.
Inner limits — the inner integral's limits are functions of the outer variable; the outer limits are always constants.

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀^{x²} (x + y) dy dx.
steps: Inner integral: ∫₀^{x²} (x + y) dy = [xy + y²/2]₀^{x²} = x³ + x⁴/2.
Outer integral: ∫₀¹ (x³ + x⁴/2) dx = 1/4 + 1/10 = 7/20.
The region is the set under y = x² and above y = 0, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀² ∫₀^{x} y dy dx.
practice.a: 4/3 (inner integral x²/2, then ∫₀² x²/2 dx).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{π} ∫₀^{sin x} y dy dx.
practice.a: π/4 (inner integral sin²x/2; ∫₀^{π} sin²x/2 dx = π/4).

lessons.takeaway: The inner limits describe the region's top and bottom (or left and right); sketch first, then integrate.

lessons.title: Double Integrals over General Regions
lessons.intro: Most regions are not rectangles: they are bounded by curves. The strategy is the same as for iterated integrals — describe the region as between two functions, then integrate across it, using 1 as the integrand when you only want the area.
concepts: Area as an integral — the area of D is ∬_D 1 dA.
Type I setup — ∬_D f dA = ∫ₐᵇ ∫_{g1(x)}^{g2(x)} f(x, y) dy dx.
Type II setup — ∬_D f dA = ∫_c^d ∫_{h1(y)}^{h2(y)} f(x, y) dx dy; pick whichever makes the limits simpler.
Intersection points — solve the boundary curves together to find where the region starts and ends.

example.q: Find the area of the region between y = x and y = x².
steps: The curves meet where x = x², i.e. x = 0 and x = 1; on [0, 1], y = x is on top.
Area = ∫₀¹ ∫_{x²}^{x} 1 dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx.

practice.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1).
Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫_{x²}^{x} (x + y) dy dx.

lessons.takeaway: Find where the boundary curves meet, integrate between them, and use f = 1 when the question is just area.

lessons.title: Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
lessons.intro: When a region is a disk, a sector, or an annulus, polar coordinates turn its boundaries into constants — but the area element changes: dA = r dr dθ, because a polar 'rectangle' grows with r.
concepts: Conversion — x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, x² + y² = r²; a disk of radius a is 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
Area element — dA = r dr dθ; never forget the extra factor of r.
When to switch — radial symmetry, circular boundaries, or integrands like x² + y² and √(x² + y²) all point to polar.
Order — usually integrate r first (inner), θ second; for a full disk the θ integral is just a factor of 2π.

example.q: Evaluate ∬_D (x² + y²) dA where D is the disk of radius 2 centered at the origin.
steps: In polar coordinates x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ; D is 0 ≤ r ≤ 2, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
The integral is ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀² r² · r dr dθ = ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀² r³ dr dθ.
Inner: ∫₀² r³ dr = 4. Outer: ∫₀^{2π} 4 dθ = 8π.

practice.q: Evaluate ∬_D √(x² + y²) dA over the unit disk.
practice.a: 2π/3 (∫₀^{2π} ∫₀¹ r² dr dθ).

practice.q: Find the area of the quarter-disk of radius 2 in the first quadrant.

lessons.takeaway: Polar coordinates: replace x² + y² by r², dA by r dr dθ, and circular boundaries become constants.

lessons.title: Triple Integrals
lessons.intro: A triple integral integrates over a solid in 3D — it gives volume when the integrand is 1, and mass when the integrand is a density. It is just an iterated integral with three layers.
concepts: Volume — the volume of a solid E is ∭_E 1 dV.
Iterated form — ∭_E f dV = ∫ ∫ ∫ f(x, y, z) dz dy dx with limits that describe E, innermost first.
Type 1 solids — between two surfaces z = u1(x, y) and z = u2(x, y) over a region D in the xy-plane.
Mass — if δ(x, y, z) is density, mass = ∭_E δ dV; center of mass divides the first moments by the mass.

example.q: Evaluate ∭_B x dV where B is the box [0, 2] × [0, 1] × [0, 1].
steps: The integral factors over the box: (∫₀² x dx)(∫₀¹ dy)(∫₀¹ dz).
∫₀² x dx = 2, and each of the other integrals is 1.
So the triple integral is 2.

practice.q: Evaluate ∭_B xyz dV over the unit cube [0, 1]³.
Evaluate ∭_B (x² + y²) dV over the unit cube [0, 1]³.
practice.a: 2/3 (∫₀¹ x² dx + ∫₀¹ y² dy = 1/3 + 1/3).

lessons.takeaway: Triple integrals are iterated integrals with three layers; 1 gives volume, density gives mass.

lessons.title: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates
lessons.intro: Cylindrical coordinates are polar coordinates with height added: (r, θ, z). They are the natural choice for solids with a circular cross-section — cylinders, cones, and anything wrapped around the z-axis.
concepts: Conversion — x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z; the volume element is dV = r dz dr dθ.
Cylinders — a solid cylinder of radius a and height h is 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ z ≤ h.
Cones — the cone z = √(x² + y²) becomes z = r, so a cone of height 1 is r ≤ z ≤ 1.
Order — usually z innermost, then r, then θ; the θ integral is often just 2π.

example.q: Find the volume of the solid cylinder of radius 2 and height 3.
steps: The cylinder is 0 ≤ r ≤ 2, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ z ≤ 3.
Volume = ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀² ∫₀³ r dz dr dθ.
Inner: ∫₀³ r dz = 3r; then ∫₀² 3r dr = 6; then ∫₀^{2π} 6 dθ = 12π — the familiar πr²h = π·4·3.

practice.q: Find the volume of the cone z = √(x² + y²) with 0 ≤ z ≤ 1.
Evaluate ∭_E z dV where E is the solid cylinder r ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ 2.
practice.a: 2π (∫₀^{2π} ∫₀¹ ∫₀² z r dz dr dθ).

lessons.takeaway: Cylindrical coordinates: keep z, go polar in xy, and never drop the r in dV = r dz dr dθ.

lessons.title: Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates
lessons.intro: Spherical coordinates describe a point by its distance ρ from the origin and two angles — φ from the positive z-axis and θ around it. They are the right tool for balls, spheres, and cones with apex at the origin.
concepts: Conversion — x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ; x² + y² + z² = ρ².
Volume element — dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ; the ρ² sin φ is the Jacobian.
Ranges — a ball of radius a is 0 ≤ ρ ≤ a, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
Cones and caps — a cone with half-angle α is 0 ≤ φ ≤ α; a spherical cap is a ≤ ρ ≤ b with φ limited.

example.q: Evaluate ∭_E √(x² + y² + z²) dV where E is the unit ball.
steps: √(x² + y² + z²) = ρ and dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ; E is 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
The integral is ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀^{π} ∫₀¹ ρ³ sin φ dρ dφ dθ.
∫₀¹ ρ³ dρ = 1/4, ∫₀^{π} sin φ dφ = 2, ∫₀^{2π} dθ = 2π, so the product is 2π · 2 · (1/4) = π.

practice.q: Find the volume of the ball of radius 2.
practice.a: 32π/3 (∫₀^{2π} ∫₀^{π} ∫₀² ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · 2 · 8/3).

practice.q: Evaluate ∭_E z² dV over the unit ball.
practice.a: 4π/15 (by symmetry it is one third of ∭ ρ² dV = 4π/5).

lessons.takeaway: Spherical coordinates: ρ for distance, φ from the z-axis, θ around it — and dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ.

lessons.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
lessons.intro: A change of variables is a substitution for double and triple integrals: it can turn a slanted parallelogram into a rectangle or an ellipse into a circle. The price is the Jacobian — the local stretching factor of the transformation.
concepts: Jacobian — for x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v), the factor is |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)|, the absolute value of the determinant of partial derivatives.
Formula — ∬_R f(x, y) dA = ∬_S f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) |∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)| du dv.
Polar and cylindrical revisited — the Jacobians r and ρ² sin φ are exactly the extra factors you already met.
Choosing the transformation — pick u and v so the region's boundaries become constants (e.g. u = x + y, v = x − y for a parallelogram).

example.q: Use the change of variables x = 2u, y = 3v to find the area of the ellipse x²/4 + y²/9 = 1.
steps: The transformation maps the ellipse to the unit disk u² + v² ≤ 1.
The Jacobian is |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = |det [[2, 0], [0, 3]]| = 6.
Area = ∬_{u²+v²≤1} 6 du dv = 6 · (area of the unit disk) = 6π.
This matches πab = π · 2 · 3.

practice.q: Find the Jacobian of x = u + v, y = u − v.
Find the Jacobian of the polar transformation x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
practice.a: r (the familiar factor in dA = r dr dθ).

lessons.takeaway: Change of variables: map the region to something simple, multiply by the Jacobian, and integrate there.

lessons.title: Vector Fields
lessons.intro: A vector field assigns a vector to every point in space — wind velocity over a map, the gravitational pull around a planet, the flow of a fluid. The two great questions about a field are whether it is a gradient (conservative) and how it curls and spreads.
concepts: Definition — F(x, y, z) = ⟨P, Q, R⟩, where P, Q, R are scalar functions; a 2D field drops the third component.
Gradient fields — F = ∇f for some potential f is called conservative; the field points in the direction of fastest increase of f.
Conservative test — on a simply connected region, F is conservative exactly when ∂P/∂y = ∂Q/∂x, ∂P/∂z = ∂R/∂x, and ∂Q/∂z = ∂R/∂y.
Finding a potential — integrate P with respect to x, then match Q and R to fix the 'constant' (a function of the other variables).

example.q: Show that F = ⟨y, x⟩ is conservative and find a potential function.
steps: Check: ∂P/∂y = 1 and ∂Q/∂x = 1 — they match, so F is conservative.
Integrate P: f = ∫ y dx = xy + g(y).
Differentiate: f_y = x + g′(y) must equal Q = x, so g′(y) = 0 and g is a constant.
Take f(x, y) = xy; indeed ∇(xy) = ⟨y, x⟩.

practice.q: Show F = ⟨x², y², z²⟩ is conservative and find a potential.
practice.a: Mixed partials all match (all are 0); f = (x³ + y³ + z³)/3.

practice.q: Is F = ⟨−y, x⟩ conservative?
practice.a: No: ∂P/∂y = −1 but ∂Q/∂x = 1.

lessons.takeaway: A field is conservative when its mixed partials match — then a potential function exists and line integrals become easy.

lessons.title: Line Integrals
lessons.intro: A line integral adds up values along a curve: a scalar function times arc length gives mass or average, while a vector field dotted with the tangent gives work — the total push of the field along the path.
concepts: Scalar line integral — ∫_C f ds = ∫ₐᵇ f(r(t)) |r′(t)| dt; ds = |r′(t)| dt is the arc-length element.
Work integral — ∫_C F · dr = ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt; this is the work done by F along C.
Parametrization — describe C by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b; reversing the direction flips the sign of a work integral but not of a scalar one.
Graphs as paths — for y = g(x), use r(t) = ⟨t, g(t)⟩.

example.q: Evaluate ∫_C y dx + x dy along the line segment from (0, 0) to (1, 1).
steps: Parametrize: r(t) = ⟨t, t⟩, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, so dx = dt and dy = dt.
On the path, y = t and x = t, so the integral is ∫₀¹ (t·1 + t·1) dt = ∫₀¹ 2t dt.
∫₀¹ 2t dt = 1.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫_C y dx along y = x² from (0, 0) to (1, 1).
practice.a: 1/3 (r(t) = ⟨t, t²⟩, dx = dt, y = t², so ∫₀¹ t² dt).

practice.q: Evaluate ∫_C (x + y) ds along the segment from (0, 0) to (1, 1).
practice.a: √2 (ds = √2 dt and x + y = 2t, so ∫₀¹ 2√2 t dt).

lessons.takeaway: Parametrize the curve, substitute, and integrate in t — ds for scalars, F · r′(t) for work.

lessons.title: Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
lessons.intro: For a conservative field, the line integral depends only on the endpoints, not the path: it is just the change in the potential function. It is the exact analogue of the single-variable fundamental theorem.
concepts: Theorem — if F = ∇f and C runs from A to B, then ∫_C F · dr = f(B) − f(A).
Path independence — a conservative field's work is the same along every path between two points.
Closed curves — the integral of a conservative field around any closed curve is 0.
Why it matters — it turns a hard path integral into two evaluations of a potential function.

example.q: Let F = ⟨2x, 2y⟩ and C be any path from (1, 0) to (0, 1). Evaluate ∫_C F · dr.
steps: F = ∇f with f(x, y) = x² + y², since ∇(x² + y²) = ⟨2x, 2y⟩.
By the fundamental theorem, the integral is f(0, 1) − f(1, 0).
f(0, 1) = 1 and f(1, 0) = 1, so the integral is 0 — as it must be for a closed loop's worth of symmetry.

practice.q: Let f(x, y) = xy and F = ∇f. Evaluate ∫_C F · dr from (0, 0) to (1, 2).
Let F = ⟨3x², 3y²⟩. Evaluate ∫_C F · dr from (0, 0) to (1, 1).
practice.a: 2 (potential f = x³ + y³; f(1, 1) − f(0, 0) = 2).

lessons.takeaway: For a gradient field, the line integral is just the potential at the end minus the potential at the start — the path does not matter.

lessons.title: Green's Theorem
lessons.intro: Green's theorem converts a line integral around a closed curve into a double integral over the region inside — trading a boundary calculation for an area calculation, or the other way around.
concepts: Circulation form — ∮_C P dx + Q dy = ∬_D (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA, for C positively (counterclockwise) oriented.
Area formula — taking P = −y/2, Q = x/2 gives area(D) = (1/2)∮_C (x dy − y dx).
Flux form — ∮_C F · n ds = ∬_D div F dA, measuring how much field flows out of D.
Orientation — the theorem needs C traversed counterclockwise; clockwise flips the sign.

example.q: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ∮_C (x dy − y dx), where C is the unit circle traversed counterclockwise.
steps: Here P = −y and Q = x, so ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2.
Green's theorem gives ∬_D 2 dA = 2 · (area of the unit disk) = 2π.
Equivalently, this is twice the area enclosed — the area formula with a factor of 2.

practice.q: Evaluate ∮_C (y dx + x dy) around the unit circle counterclockwise.
Evaluate ∮_C x² dy around the unit circle counterclockwise.
practice.a: 0 (the double integral is ∬_D 2x dA, which is 0 by symmetry).

lessons.takeaway: Green's theorem: the circulation around the boundary equals the double integral of (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) over the inside.

lessons.title: Curl and Divergence
lessons.intro: Curl measures a field's local rotation — how much it swirls around a point — and divergence measures its local outflow — whether the point is a source or a sink. Together they are the two derivatives that matter for vector fields.
concepts: Curl — ∇ × F = ⟨∂R/∂y − ∂Q/∂z, ∂P/∂z − ∂R/∂x, ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y⟩; it is a vector pointing along the axis of rotation.
Divergence — div F = ∇ · F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z; it is a scalar, positive at sources and negative at sinks.
Conservative fields — F = ∇f has curl 0; conversely, a curl-free field on a simply connected region is conservative.
Identities — div(curl F) = 0 and curl(∇f) = 0 always.

example.q: Find the curl and divergence of F = ⟨−y, x, 0⟩.
steps: Divergence: ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 — the field neither spreads nor compresses.
The field rotates counterclockwise about the z-axis with twice the unit angular speed — as expected for solid-body rotation.

practice.q: Find div and curl of F = ⟨x², y², z²⟩.
practice.a: div F = 2x + 2y + 2z; curl F = ⟨0, 0, 0⟩.

practice.q: Find div and curl of F = ⟨yz, xz, xy⟩.
practice.a: div F = 0; curl F = ⟨0, 0, 0⟩ (it is the gradient of xyz).

lessons.takeaway: Curl is the swirl (a vector), divergence is the source strength (a scalar); gradient fields have zero curl.

lessons.title: Surface Integrals
lessons.intro: A surface integral adds up values over a curved surface — mass of a shell, flux of a field through it. The key is the surface area element dS, which measures how a parametrization stretches area.
concepts: Scalar surface integral — ∬_S f dS = ∬_D f(r(u,v)) |r_u × r_v| du dv.
Graphs — for z = g(x, y), dS = √(1 + g_x² + g_y²) dA.
Flux — ∬_S F · dS = ∬_S F · n dS measures the flow of F through S; the orientation (choice of n) fixes the sign.
Closed surfaces — outward is the standard orientation for flux out of a solid.

example.q: Evaluate ∬_S z dS where S is the part of the plane z = 1 − x − y in the first octant.
steps: On the plane, g_x = g_y = −1, so dS = √(1 + 1 + 1) dA = √3 dA.
The projection D is the triangle x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 1.

practice.q: Find the surface area of the cone z = √(x² + y²) with 0 ≤ z ≤ 1.
practice.a: √2 π (dS = √2 dA over the unit disk).

practice.q: Find the flux of F = ⟨x, y, z⟩ outward through the unit sphere.
practice.a: 4π (on the sphere F · n = 1, so the flux is the sphere's area).

lessons.takeaway: Surface integrals need dS: for a graph, √(1 + g_x² + g_y²) dA; flux dots the field with the unit normal.

lessons.title: Stokes' Theorem
lessons.intro: Stokes' theorem says the circulation of a field around a closed curve equals the flux of its curl through any surface the curve bounds. It is Green's theorem lifted off the plane and into space.
concepts: Theorem — ∮_C F · dr = ∬_S (∇ × F) · n dS, where C is the boundary of S with compatible orientation (right-hand rule).
Choose the easiest surface — any surface with the same boundary works, so pick a flat disk when you can.
Orientation — curl your right-hand fingers along C and your thumb gives the normal direction for S.
Physical meaning — the total swirl through a surface is measured by the circulation around its rim.

example.q: Verify Stokes' theorem for F = ⟨−y, x, 0⟩ with C the unit circle in the xy-plane and S the unit disk.
steps: Line integral: parametrize x = cos t, y = sin t. Then −y dx + x dy = sin²t dt + cos²t dt = dt, so ∮_C F · dr = ∫₀^{2π} dt = 2π.
Curl: ∇ × F = ⟨0, 0, 2⟩, and n = ⟨0, 0, 1⟩ on the disk.
Surface integral: ∬_S ⟨0, 0, 2⟩ · ⟨0, 0, 1⟩ dS = ∬_S 2 dS = 2π — the two sides agree.

practice.q: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate ∮_C F · dr for F = ⟨0, x, 0⟩ around the unit circle in the xy-plane.
practice.a: π (curl F = ⟨0, 0, 1⟩, flux through the disk is its area π).

practice.q: For F = ⟨z, x, y⟩, find the flux of curl F through the unit disk in the xy-plane.
practice.a: π (curl F = ⟨1, 1, 1⟩; its z-component is 1, so the flux is the disk's area).

lessons.takeaway: Circulation around the rim equals the flux of the curl through the surface — and you may choose the simplest surface with that rim.

lessons.title: Divergence Theorem
lessons.intro: The divergence theorem — Gauss's theorem — says the flux of a field out of a closed surface equals the triple integral of its divergence over the solid inside. It is the 3D version of Green's flux form and the capstone of the course.
concepts: Theorem — ∬_S F · dS = ∭_E div F dV, where S is the closed boundary of the solid E, oriented outward.
When to use it — flux through a complicated closed surface becomes a (usually easier) volume integral.
Sources and sinks — div F > 0 means the field is created inside E; div F < 0 means it is absorbed.
Relation to the others — the fundamental theorem, Green's, Stokes', and the divergence theorem are all one idea: the integral over a boundary equals the integral of a derivative over the inside.

example.q: Verify the divergence theorem for F = ⟨x, y, z⟩ over the unit ball.
steps: Divergence: div F = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so ∭_E 3 dV = 3 · (volume of the unit ball) = 3 · (4π/3) = 4π.
Flux: on the unit sphere the outward unit normal is n = ⟨x, y, z⟩, so F · n = x² + y² + z² = 1.
∬_S 1 dS = the sphere's surface area = 4π — the two sides agree.

practice.q: Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of F = ⟨2x, 2y, 2z⟩ out of the unit cube [0, 1]³.
practice.a: 6 (div F = 6, and the cube's volume is 1).

practice.q: Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of F = ⟨x³, y³, z³⟩ out of the unit sphere.
practice.a: 12π/5 (div F = 3(x² + y² + z²) = 3ρ²; ∭ 3ρ² dV = 12π/5).

lessons.takeaway: Flux out of a closed surface equals the triple integral of the divergence inside — the grand finale of vector calculus.

MATH201.mastery_rubric: To pass, students must demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of multivariable functions, partial differentiation, and multiple integration. Proficiency in vector calculus, including line and surface integrals, and the application of Green's, Stokes', and Divergence Theorems is required. Final course grade must be 70% or higher, with at least 60% on the final exam.

lessons.title: Definitions and Terminology
lessons.intro: A differential equation is an equation that involves an unknown function and its derivatives. The whole course is about recognizing what kind of equation you have — its order, whether it is linear, and what a solution means — because the type of the equation decides the method that solves it.
concepts: Order — the order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative in it; y'' + 3y' + y = 0 is second order.

Linear vs. nonlinear — an equation is linear if the unknown function and its derivatives appear only to the first power, with no products of them; (y'')² + y = 0 is nonlinear because of the squared derivative, and y·y' = x is nonlinear because of the product.

Solution — a function is a solution on an interval if substituting it (and its derivatives) into the equation makes it a true identity there; most equations have a whole family of solutions, one for each choice of the arbitrary constants.
General vs. particular solution — the general solution contains arbitrary constants (as many as the order); a particular solution is one member of the family, picked out by extra conditions.

example.q: Show that y = e^{3x} is a solution of y'' − 9y = 0, and state the order of the equation and whether it is linear.
steps: Differentiate: y' = 3e^{3x} and y'' = 9e^{3x}.
Substitute: y'' − 9y = 9e^{3x} − 9e^{3x} = 0, so the identity holds for every x.
The highest derivative is y'', so the equation is second order; y and y'' appear only to the first power, so it is linear.
example.a: y = e^{3x} is a solution; the equation is second order and linear

practice.q: Give the order of (y'')² + y' = sin x, and say whether it is linear or nonlinear.
practice.a: Second order; nonlinear, because y'' is squared.

practice.q: Verify that y = sin x + cos x is a solution of y'' + y = 0.
practice.a: y' = cos x − sin x, y'' = −sin x − cos x = −y, so y'' + y = 0.

lessons.takeaway: Order is the highest derivative present; linear means no powers or products of the unknown function and its derivatives.

lessons.title: Initial-Value Problems
lessons.intro: A differential equation alone usually has infinitely many solutions. An initial-value problem (IVP) pins down one of them by prescribing the value of the function (and its derivatives, for higher order) at a single point — the starting state of the system.
concepts: Initial conditions — for a first-order equation one condition y(x0) = y0 is enough; an n-th order equation needs n conditions, y(x0), y'(x0), …, y^{(n−1)}(x0).
How to solve an IVP — find the general solution first, then use the initial conditions to solve for the constants; do the algebra at the end, not inside the integration.

Existence and uniqueness — for y' = f(x, y) with f and ∂f/∂y continuous near (x0, y0), the IVP has exactly one solution through that point; a solution can still fail to exist if the equation blows up, as with y' = y², y(0) = 1 at x = 1.
Why it matters — an IVP is the mathematical form of a physical prediction: the equation is the law, the initial condition is the state of the world now.

example.q: Solve the initial-value problem dy/dx = 2x with y(1) = 3.
steps: Integrate: y = ∫ 2x dx = x² + C, the general solution.
Apply the initial condition: y(1) = 1 + C = 3, so C = 2.
The particular solution is y = x² + 2.

practice.q: Solve dy/dx = 3x² with y(0) = 1.
practice.a: y = x³ + 1 (since y = x³ + C and C = 1).

practice.q: Solve y'' = 6x with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 2.
practice.a: y = x³ + 2x + 1 (integrate twice: y' = 3x² + 2, then y = x³ + 2x + 1).

lessons.takeaway: Solve generally first, then use the initial conditions to fix the constants — one condition per order of the equation.

lessons.title: Differential Equations as Mathematical Models
lessons.intro: Differential equations are how change is written down: a rate of change depends on the present state, and that dependence is the equation. Population growth, cooling, decay, and motion all become first-order equations once you translate the words into a rate.
concepts: Proportional growth — if a quantity grows at a rate proportional to itself, dP/dt = kP, the solution is exponential, P = P0 e^{kt}; k > 0 is growth, k < 0 is decay.
Newton's law of cooling — the rate of change of temperature is proportional to the difference from the surroundings: dT/dt = k(T − Tm), solved by T = Tm + (T0 − Tm) e^{kt}.
Radioactive decay and half-life — dN/dt = −λN gives N = N0 e^{−λt}; the half-life is the time for N to halve, ln 2 / λ.
Building the model — name the quantity, write its rate as a function of the quantity itself and time, and check the units: a rate of grams per minute must equal grams per minute on both sides.

example.q: A cup of coffee is 90°C in a 20°C room. After 10 minutes it has cooled to 60°C. What is its temperature after 20 minutes?
steps: Model: dT/dt = k(T − 20), so T(t) = 20 + 70 e^{kt}.

practice.q: A bacterial culture starts with 500 cells and doubles every 4 hours. How many cells are there after 12 hours?
practice.a: 4,000 (three doublings: 500 · 2³).

practice.q: A radioactive sample has half-life 10 days and starts at 800 g. How much remains after 30 days?
practice.a: 100 g (three half-lives: 800 / 2³).

lessons.takeaway: Translate a rate statement into d(quantity)/dt = (function of the quantity); proportional rates give exponentials.

lessons.title: Solution Curves
lessons.intro: Before solving an equation, you can see its solutions: at every point (x, y) the equation dy/dx = f(x, y) prescribes a slope, and the solutions are the curves that follow those slopes everywhere. The picture of all the little slope segments is the direction field.
concepts: Direction field — at each point (x, y) draw a short segment of slope f(x, y); solution curves are tangent to the segments they pass through, so you can sketch a solution by following the field.
Isoclines — curves f(x, y) = c along which all slopes are equal to c; for dy/dx = x + y the isocline of slope 1 is the line y = 1 − x.
Reading equilibrium — where f(x, y) = 0 the slope is zero, so solutions flatten there; a horizontal line y = y0 with f(x, y0) = 0 is a constant (equilibrium) solution.
When the field is enough — the field shows the qualitative behavior (growth, decay, oscillation) even when no closed-form solution exists, which is most of the time in real applications.

example.q: For dy/dx = 2x, find the slope of the direction field at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (−1, 1), and describe the solution curves.
steps: The slope depends only on x: at (0, 0) the slope is 2·0 = 0; at (1, 0) it is 2; at (−1, 1) it is −2.
A curve following these slopes must flatten at x = 0 and rise steeply for large |x|.
Solving gives y = x² + C — parabolas, one through each initial point, exactly as the field suggests.
example.a: Slopes 0, 2, −2; solution curves are the parabolas y = x² + C

practice.q: For dy/dx = y, what is the slope of the direction field at (0, 1) and at (1, 2)?
practice.a: 1 at (0, 1) and 2 at (1, 2) — the slope equals the y-coordinate.

practice.q: For dy/dx = x + y, find the isocline where the slope equals 1.
practice.a: The line x + y = 1, i.e. y = 1 − x.

lessons.takeaway: The direction field turns an equation into a picture: solutions are the curves tangent to the slope segments everywhere.

lessons.title: Separable Equations
lessons.intro: A first-order equation is separable when it can be rearranged so that all the y's (with dy) sit on one side and all the x's (with dx) on the other. Then both sides integrate independently — it is the simplest solving method, and the first one to try.
concepts: The test — dy/dx = g(x) h(y) is separable; dy/dx = x + y is not, because the right side cannot be factored into a function of x times a function of y.
The procedure — write dy/h(y) = g(x) dx, integrate both sides, and solve for y when you can; a single constant of integration is enough, since the two constants combine into one.
Lost solutions — dividing by h(y) can throw away constant solutions where h(y) = 0; check those separately (for dy/dx = y², the solution y = 0 is lost by the division).
Choosing the branch — after integrating you often get y² = something; the initial condition picks the sign of the square root.

example.q: Solve dy/dx = x/y with y(0) = 2.
steps: Separate: y dy = x dx.
Integrate: y²/2 = x²/2 + C, so y² = x² + 2C; rename 2C as C.
Apply y(0) = 2: 4 = 0 + C, so C = 4 and y² = x² + 4; the initial value is positive, so y = √(x² + 4).

practice.q: Solve dy/dx = e^x / y with y(0) = 1.
Solve dy/dx = y/x with y(1) = 2.
practice.a: y = 2x (from ln|y| = ln|x| + C).

lessons.takeaway: Factor the right side into g(x)·h(y), separate, integrate both sides — and check for constant solutions lost by division.

lessons.title: Linear Equations
lessons.intro: A first-order linear equation, y' + P(x) y = Q(x), can always be solved by one trick: multiply by an integrating factor that turns the left side into the derivative of a single product. No guessing is needed — the method works for every linear equation.
concepts: Standard form — divide through so the equation reads y' + P(x) y = Q(x); P and Q are the two functions you need.
Integrating factor — μ(x) = e^{∫P(x) dx}; multiplying by μ makes the left side exactly d/dx(μ y), because μ' = P μ.
The solve — d/dx(μ y) = μ Q, so μ y = ∫ μ Q dx + C, and y = (∫ μ Q dx + C)/μ; the integral of μ Q is the only hard step.
Homogeneous vs. nonhomogeneous — with Q = 0 the solution is y = C e^{−∫P dx}; the general solution is that homogeneous part plus any one particular solution.

example.q: Solve y' + 2y = e^x.
steps: Standard form is already there with P(x) = 2, so μ = e^{∫2 dx} = e^{2x}.
Multiply: d/dx(e^{2x} y) = e^{2x} · e^x = e^{3x}.
Integrate: e^{2x} y = e^{3x}/3 + C, so y = e^x/3 + C e^{−2x}.

practice.q: Solve y' − y = 2 with y(0) = 1.
Solve xy' + y = x².
practice.a: y = x²/3 + C/x (divide by x: y' + y/x = x, μ = x, so d/dx(xy) = x²).

lessons.takeaway: Linear first-order equations always yield to the integrating factor μ = e^{∫P dx}: the left side becomes d/dx(μ y).

lessons.title: Exact Equations
lessons.intro: Some equations M(x, y) dx + N(x, y) dy = 0 are secretly the total differential of one function F(x, y) — the equation is just dF = 0, so the solution is F(x, y) = C. The test for that is one partial-derivative equality.
concepts: The exactness test — M dx + N dy is exact (equals dF for some F) exactly when ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, on a simply connected region.
Finding F — integrate M with respect to x (treating y as constant) to get F = ∫M dx + h(y), then use ∂F/∂y = N to find h'(y) and h(y).
The solution — once F is found, the implicit solution is F(x, y) = C; you rarely need to solve for y explicitly.

If the test fails — the equation is not exact as written, but sometimes multiplying by an integrating factor (often a function of x alone or y alone) makes it exact; linear equations are the classic case.

example.q: Solve (2xy + 1) dx + (x² + 3y²) dy = 0.
steps: Test: ∂M/∂y = 2x and ∂N/∂x = 2x — equal, so the equation is exact.
Integrate M in x: F = ∫(2xy + 1) dx = x²y + x + h(y).
∂F/∂y = x² + h'(y) must equal N = x² + 3y², so h'(y) = 3y² and h(y) = y³.
The solution is F = C.

practice.q: Solve (3x² + y) dx + (x + 2y) dy = 0.
practice.a: x³ + xy + y² = C (exact: ∂M/∂y = 1 = ∂N/∂x).

practice.q: Show y dx + (x + 1) dy = 0 is exact and solve it.
practice.a: xy + y = C (∂M/∂y = 1 = ∂N/∂x; F = xy + y).

lessons.takeaway: Check ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x; if it holds, integrate M in x, fix the leftover function of y with N, and set F = C.

lessons.title: Homogeneous Equations
lessons.intro: A first-order equation is homogeneous when its right side depends only on the ratio y/x — the equation looks the same at every scale. The substitution v = y/x collapses it into a separable equation in v and x.
concepts: The test — M(x, y) and N(x, y) are homogeneous of the same degree n if M(tx, ty) = tⁿ M(x, y); then dy/dx = −M/N depends only on y/x.
The substitution — set y = v x, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx; the equation becomes separable in v and x.
Back-substitution — after solving for v, replace v by y/x to get the implicit solution in x and y.
Why it works — scaling (x, y) → (tx, ty) leaves the direction field unchanged along each ray through the origin, so the field is determined by the slope y/x alone.

example.q: Solve dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy).
steps: The right side is (x/y) + (y/x), a function of y/x only — homogeneous. Set y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx and the equation becomes v + x dv/dx = 1/v + v.
Cancel v and separate: x dv/dx = 1/v, so v dv = dx/x.
Integrate: v²/2 = ln|x| + C. Back-substitute v = y/x.

practice.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/x.
practice.a: y = x ln|x| + Cx (v = y/x gives x dv/dx = 1).

practice.q: Solve dy/dx = y/x + x/y.
practice.a: y² = 2x² ln|x| + Cx² (v dv = dx/x with v = y/x).

lessons.takeaway: If the right side depends only on y/x, set y = vx — the equation separates in v and x.

lessons.title: Applications of First-Order Equations
lessons.intro: The first-order methods now become models of real systems: a tank filling and draining, a circuit charging, a family of curves and the curves that cross it at right angles. The equation is built the same way every time — rate in minus rate out.
concepts: Mixing — for a tank of volume V with concentration, dA/dt = (rate in) − (rate out) = (inflow rate)(inflow concentration) − (outflow rate)(A/V); with equal in/out flow it is linear with constant coefficients.
Orthogonal trajectories — given a family F(x, y, C) = 0, differentiate and eliminate C to get the family's differential equation, then replace y' by −1/y' and solve for the perpendicular family.
RC circuits — charge q on a capacitor satisfies R dq/dt + q/C = E(t); it is a linear equation whose steady state is q = C·E.
The pattern — every application is the same move: name the changing quantity, write its rate as inflow minus outflow (or force divided by mass), and solve the resulting first-order equation.

example.q: A 100-liter tank starts with pure water. Brine with 5 g/L of salt flows in at 2 L/min, and the well-mixed solution flows out at 2 L/min. How much salt is in the tank after 50 minutes?
steps: Let A(t) be grams of salt. Salt enters at 2·5 = 10 g/min and leaves at 2·(A/100) g/min, so dA/dt = 10 − A/50, A(0) = 0.
Linear with μ = e^{t/50}: d/dt(e^{t/50} A) = 10 e^{t/50}, so A = 500 + C e^{−t/50}; A(0) = 0 gives C = −500.
example.a: About 316 g (the tank tends toward 500 g)

practice.q: A circuit has R = 10 Ω, C = 0.01 F, and a constant 5 V source. What charge does the capacitor approach in the long run?
practice.a: 0.05 C (steady state q = C·E = 0.01·5).

practice.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family y = Cx².
practice.a: x² + 2y² = C (ellipses: the family has y' = 2y/x, so the orthogonal family has y' = −x/(2y)).

lessons.takeaway: Rate in minus rate out builds the equation; the first-order methods then finish the job.

lessons.title: Preliminary Theory: Linear Equations
lessons.intro: Second-order linear equations behave like first-order ones, one level up: the solutions form a two-dimensional vector space, and two independent solutions are all you ever need. The Wronskian is the test that tells you whether two solutions are genuinely different.
concepts: Superposition — if y1 and y2 solve a homogeneous linear equation, so does every combination C1 y1 + C2 y2; the solution set is a vector space of dimension equal to the order.

Linear independence — y1 and y2 are independent if neither is a constant multiple of the other; for solutions of a linear equation, independence on an interval is equivalent to a nonzero Wronskian there.
Wronskian — W(y1, y2) = y1 y2' − y1' y2; Abel's identity says W(x) = C e^{−∫P(x) dx} for y'' + P(x) y' + Q(x) y = 0, so it is either always zero or never zero.
Existence and uniqueness — if P, Q, and the forcing term are continuous on an interval containing x0, the IVP with y(x0) and y'(x0) given has exactly one solution on that interval.

example.q: Are y1 = e^x and y2 = e^{2x} linearly independent? Compute their Wronskian.
steps: That is 2e^{3x} − e^{3x} = e^{3x}.
e^{3x} is never zero, so the Wronskian never vanishes and the functions are linearly independent on every interval.
example.a: W = e^{3x} ≠ 0, so y1 and y2 are linearly independent

practice.q: Compute the Wronskian of sin x and cos x. Are they independent?
practice.a: W = sin x·(−sin x) − cos x·cos x = −1 ≠ 0, so they are independent.

practice.q: Compute the Wronskian of y1 = x and y2 = x². Where are they independent?
practice.a: W = x·2x − 1·x² = x², nonzero for x ≠ 0, so they are independent on (0, ∞) (and on (−∞, 0)).

lessons.takeaway: Two solutions span the whole solution space exactly when their Wronskian is nonzero.

lessons.title: Reduction of Order
lessons.intro: If you know one solution of a homogeneous second-order linear equation, you can find a second one: look for it in the form y2 = u(x) y1(x). The equation for u collapses to first order — the order is reduced, hence the name.
concepts: The ansatz — set y2 = u y1; substituting into the equation kills the u term (because y1 is a solution), leaving a first-order equation for u'.
The formula — y2 = y1 ∫ e^{−∫P(x) dx} / y1² dx for y'' + P(x) y' + Q(x) y = 0; any one antiderivative will do, since adding a constant just adds a multiple of y1.
When to use it — whenever one solution is obvious (a constant, an exponential, a polynomial) and the equation has non-constant coefficients so the constant-coefficient method does not apply.
It always works — reduction of order never fails for a second-order linear equation; the only risk is that the integral for u is hard to evaluate in closed form.

example.q: Given that y1 = e^{2x} solves y'' − 4y' + 4y = 0, find a second independent solution.
steps: Here P(x) = −4, so e^{−∫P dx} = e^{4x}.
Taking the antiderivative x gives y2 = x e^{2x}, which is independent of e^{2x}.
example.a: y2 = x e^{2x}; the general solution is (C1 + C2 x) e^{2x}

practice.q: Given y1 = 1 solves y'' − y' = 0, find a second solution by reduction of order.
practice.a: y2 = e^x (P = −1, so y2 = ∫ e^x dx = e^x).

practice.q: Given y1 = cos x solves y'' + y = 0, find a second solution.
practice.a: y2 = sin x (P = 0, so y2 = cos x ∫ dx/cos²x = cos x tan x = sin x).

lessons.takeaway: One known solution gives a second: y2 = y1 ∫ e^{−∫P dx}/y1² dx.

lessons.title: Homogeneous Linear Equations with Constant Coefficients
lessons.intro: With constant coefficients, exponentials are the key: try y = e^{mx} and the differential equation becomes an algebraic one — the auxiliary (characteristic) equation. Its roots, real or complex, repeated or distinct, write down the whole solution space.
concepts: The auxiliary equation — substituting y = e^{mx} into a y'' + b y' + c y = 0 gives (a m² + b m + c) e^{mx} = 0, so m must satisfy a m² + b m + c = 0.
Distinct real roots — m1 ≠ m2 gives y = C1 e^{m1 x} + C2 e^{m2 x}.
Repeated root — m1 = m2 = m gives y = (C1 + C2 x) e^{mx}; the extra factor x comes from reduction of order.
Complex roots — m = α ± βi gives y = e^{αx} (C1 cos βx + C2 sin βx); the real and imaginary parts of e^{(α+βi)x} are the two real solutions.

example.q: Solve y'' − 5y' + 6y = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 0.
steps: Auxiliary equation: m² − 5m + 6 = 0, so (m − 2)(m − 3) = 0 and m = 2, 3.
General solution: y = C1 e^{2x} + C2 e^{3x}; y' = 2C1 e^{2x} + 3C2 e^{3x}.
y(0) = C1 + C2 = 1 and y'(0) = 2C1 + 3C2 = 0; solving gives C1 = 3, C2 = −2.

practice.q: Solve y'' + 4y' + 4y = 0.
practice.a: y = (C1 + C2 x) e^{−2x} (repeated root m = −2).

practice.q: Solve y'' − 2y' + 5y = 0.
practice.a: y = e^x (C1 cos 2x + C2 sin 2x) (roots 1 ± 2i).

lessons.takeaway: Try e^{mx}: the auxiliary equation's roots give the solution — distinct roots give exponentials, a repeat adds an x, complex roots give e^{αx} times sine and cosine.

lessons.title: Undetermined Coefficients (Superposition Approach)
lessons.intro: For a constant-coefficient equation with a forcing term built from polynomials, exponentials, sines, and cosines, the particular solution has the same shape as the forcing term — with unknown coefficients to determine. Guess the shape, plug in, and solve for the coefficients.
concepts: The guess table — for forcing e^{ax} try A e^{ax}; for a polynomial of degree n try a polynomial of degree n; for sin bx or cos bx try A cos bx + B sin bx; for products, multiply the guesses.
The resonance rule — if any term of your guess already solves the homogeneous equation, multiply that part of the guess by x (and by x again if the root is repeated).
Superposition — a forcing term that is a sum gets a particular solution that is the sum of the particular solutions for each piece; solve each piece separately.
Why it works — differentiating a polynomial, exponential, or sinusoid stays in the same family, so the equation can only match the forcing term if the guess has the same shape.

example.q: Solve y'' − 3y' + 2y = e^{3x}.
steps: Homogeneous: m² − 3m + 2 = 0 gives m = 1, 2, so y_h = C1 e^x + C2 e^{2x}.
e^{3x} is not a homogeneous solution, so try y_p = A e^{3x}. Then y_p' = 3A e^{3x}, y_p'' = 9A e^{3x}.
Substitute: 9A − 9A + 2A = 2A must equal 1, so A = 1/2.

practice.q: Find a particular solution of y'' + y = sin x.
practice.a: y_p = −(x/2) cos x (sin x is a homogeneous solution, so multiply the guess by x).

practice.q: Find a particular solution of y'' − y = 2x.
practice.a: y_p = −2x (try Ax + B: −Ax − B = 2x gives A = −2, B = 0).

lessons.takeaway: Guess the forcing term's shape with unknown coefficients; multiply by x when the guess collides with a homogeneous solution.

lessons.title: Variation of Parameters
lessons.intro: Undetermined coefficients only works for special forcing terms. Variation of parameters works for any forcing term: take the homogeneous solutions y1, y2 and let their constants vary with x, then solve a small linear system for the derivatives of those varying constants.
concepts: The ansatz — seek y_p = u1(x) y1 + u2(x) y2 with the constraint u1' y1 + u2' y2 = 0, which keeps y_p' free of u1'' and u2''.
The system — u1' y1 + u2' y2 = 0 and u1' y1' + u2' y2' = g(x) (the forcing term), solved by Cramer's rule with the Wronskian: u1' = −y2 g/W, u2' = y1 g/W.
Integrate and assemble — integrate u1' and u2' (any antiderivatives; constants of integration just add homogeneous solutions), then y_p = u1 y1 + u2 y2.
When to use it — any forcing term, especially ones undetermined coefficients cannot touch, like sec x, ln x, or 1/(1 + x²); the price is that the integrals may be hard.

example.q: Find a particular solution of y'' + y = sec x.
steps: Homogeneous solutions: y1 = cos x, y2 = sin x, with Wronskian W = 1.
u1' = −y2 g/W = −sin x sec x = −tan x, so u1 = ln|cos x|; u2' = y1 g/W = cos x sec x = 1, so u2 = x.
Assemble: y_p = u1 y1 + u2 y2 = cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x.
example.a: y_p = cos x · ln|cos x| + x sin x

practice.q: Find a particular solution of y'' − y = e^x by variation of parameters.
Find a particular solution of y'' + 4y = 1 by variation of parameters.
practice.a: y_p = 1/4 (u1' = −sin 2x / 2, u2' = cos 2x / 2; the pieces combine to the constant 1/4).

lessons.takeaway: Let the constants vary: u1' = −y2 g/W and u2' = y1 g/W, integrate, and y_p = u1 y1 + u2 y2 — it works for any forcing term.

lessons.title: Cauchy-Euler Equation
lessons.intro: The Cauchy-Euler (equidimensional) equation x² y'' + a x y' + b y = 0 has variable coefficients, but a power ansatz y = x^m turns it into algebra again — the same trick as constant coefficients, with x^m playing the role of e^{mx}.
concepts: The indicial equation — substituting y = x^m gives m(m − 1) + a m + b = 0, a quadratic for m.
Distinct real roots — m1 ≠ m2 gives y = C1 x^{m1} + C2 x^{m2}.
Repeated root — m1 = m2 = m gives y = (C1 + C2 ln x) x^m; the logarithm is the Euler analogue of the extra factor x.
Complex roots — m = α ± βi gives y = x^α (C1 cos(β ln x) + C2 sin(β ln x)); the oscillation lives in ln x, not in x.

example.q: Solve x² y'' − 3x y' + 4y = 0 for x > 0.
steps: Repeated root m = 2, so the solutions are x² and x² ln x.
General solution: y = (C1 + C2 ln x) x².

practice.q: Solve x² y'' + 3x y' + y = 0.
practice.a: y = (C1 + C2 ln x)/x (indicial (m+1)² = 0).

practice.q: Solve x² y'' + x y' − y = 0.
practice.a: y = C1 x + C2/x (indicial m² − 1 = 0).

lessons.takeaway: Try y = x^m: the indicial quadratic's roots give the solution — a repeat adds ln x, complex roots give sine and cosine of ln x.

lessons.title: Definition of the Laplace Transform
lessons.intro: The Laplace transform converts a function of time into a function of a new variable s, turning differentiation into multiplication by s. Differential equations become algebraic equations — solve those, then transform back.
concepts: The definition — L{f(t)} = ∫_0^∞ e^{−st} f(t) dt, defined when the integral converges (for s large enough); linearity holds, L{af + bg} = aL{f} + bL{g}.
Basic transforms — L{1} = 1/s, L{e^{at}} = 1/(s − a) for s > a, L{tⁿ} = n!/s^{n+1}, L{sin at} = a/(s² + a²), L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²).
The key property — L{f'} = s F(s) − f(0) and L{f''} = s² F(s) − s f(0) − f'(0): initial conditions enter automatically, which is why the transform is made for IVPs.
Existence — functions of exponential order (bounded by Me^{ct}) have a transform for s > c; a jump discontinuity is fine, but e^{t²} grows too fast and has no Laplace transform.

example.q: Compute L{e^{2t}} from the definition.
steps: The antiderivative is −e^{−(s−2)t}/(s−2); at the upper limit it vanishes only when s > 2.
At t = 0 the value is 1/(s − 2).

practice.q: Find L{t²}.
practice.a: 2/s³ (integrate by parts twice, or use n!/s^{n+1} with n = 2).

practice.q: Find L{sin 3t}.

lessons.takeaway: L{f} = ∫_0^∞ e^{−st} f(t) dt; differentiation becomes multiplication by s, with the initial values built in.

lessons.title: Inverse Transforms
lessons.intro: After solving in the s-domain, you must come back: the inverse Laplace transform turns F(s) into f(t). In practice this is pattern-matching against the transform table, using partial fractions to break complicated rational functions into recognizable pieces.
concepts: Table lookup — 1/(s − a) inverts to e^{at}, s/(s² + a²) to cos at, a/(s² + a²) to sin at, n!/s^{n+1} to tⁿ.
Partial fractions — a rational F(s) splits into terms like A/(s − a) and (Bs + C)/(s² + a²); each piece inverts by the table, and the pieces add.
Uniqueness — if two continuous functions have the same Laplace transform, they are the same function, so the inverse is well defined.
Completing the square — denominators like s² + 2s + 5 become (s + 1)² + 4, which inverts (with the shift theorem) to e^{−t} times sine or cosine.

steps: Partial fractions: 1/((s − 1)(s − 2)) = A/(s − 1) + B/(s − 2). Setting s = 1 gives 1 = −A, so A = −1; setting s = 2 gives 1 = B, so B = 1.
So the transform is −1/(s − 1) + 1/(s − 2).
Invert term by term: −e^t + e^{2t}.

practice.a: sin 2t (it is 2/(s² + 2²)).
1 − e^{−t} (partial fractions give 1/s − 1/(s + 1)).

lessons.takeaway: Invert by partial fractions plus the table: split F(s) into pieces you recognize, invert each one, and add.

lessons.title: Operational Properties I & II
lessons.intro: Two translation theorems make the Laplace transform flexible: multiplying by an exponential in time shifts the transform in s, and delaying a function in time multiplies its transform by an exponential in s. Together with the derivative of a transform, they handle almost every transform you meet.
concepts: First translation (s-shift) — L{e^{at} f(t)} = F(s − a): an exponential factor slides the transform sideways; e^{−t} cos 2t transforms to (s + 1)/((s + 1)² + 4).
Second translation (t-shift) — L{f(t − a) U(t − a)} = e^{−as} F(s), where U is the unit step: a delayed function gets an exponential factor.
Derivative of a transform — L{t f(t)} = −F'(s); multiplying by t in the time domain is differentiating (with a minus sign) in the s-domain.
Unit step — U(t − a) is 0 before a and 1 after; L{U(t − a)} = e^{−as}/s, the workhorse for piecewise forcing.

example.q: Find L{e^{−2t} cos 3t}.
steps: Start with L{cos 3t} = s/(s² + 9).
Multiplying by e^{−2t} shifts s to s + 2 (first translation, a = −2).
Replace every s by s + 2: (s + 2)/((s + 2)² + 9).

practice.a: e^{−t} cos 2t (reverse the s-shift with a = −1).

practice.q: Find L{t e^{3t}}.
practice.a: 1/(s − 3)² (differentiate L{e^{3t}} = 1/(s − 3) and negate).

lessons.takeaway: e^{at} in time shifts s; a delay in time multiplies by e^{−as}; a factor t differentiates the transform.

lessons.title: Dirac Delta Function
lessons.intro: A hammer blow, a sudden impulse, a force that acts for an instant: the Dirac delta δ(t − a) models a unit impulse concentrated at one instant. It is not an ordinary function — it is zero everywhere except at t = a, where it is infinitely tall — but its Laplace transform is clean, and it makes impulse problems solvable.
concepts: The defining property — ∫_0^∞ δ(t − a) f(t) dt = f(a): the delta sifts out the value of f at a; in particular ∫ δ = 1, a unit impulse.
Laplace transform — L{δ(t − a)} = e^{−as} (and L{δ(t)} = 1): an impulse in time is just a delay factor in the s-domain.

Solving impulse IVPs — transform the equation, solve algebraically for Y(s), and invert with the second translation theorem; the response is zero until the impulse hits, then a shifted copy of the natural response.
Physical meaning — the response to δ(t − a) is the impulse response of the system: a mass-spring system hit at time a starts oscillating from that instant with amplitude set by the system.

example.q: Solve y'' + y = δ(t − 2π) with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 0.
steps: Transform: (s² + 1) Y(s) = e^{−2πs}, so Y(s) = e^{−2πs}/(s² + 1).
1/(s² + 1) inverts to sin t, and the factor e^{−2πs} delays it by 2π: y = sin(t − 2π) U(t − 2π).
Since sin(t − 2π) = sin t, the response is 0 until t = 2π and then sin t.
example.a: y(t) = 0 for t < 2π, y(t) = sin t for t > 2π

practice.q: Find L{δ(t − 3)}.
Solve y'' + 4y = δ(t − 1) with y(0) = y'(0) = 0.

lessons.takeaway: δ(t − a) is a unit impulse at time a; its transform is e^{−as}, and the response is the natural response delayed to a.

lessons.title: Systems of Linear Differential Equations
lessons.intro: Many real systems are coupled: two tanks, two species, a mass on two springs. The Laplace transform solves a whole system at once — transform every equation, solve the resulting algebraic system for the transforms, and invert each one.
concepts: Transform each equation — L{x'} = sX − x(0) for every unknown, so a system of n first-order equations becomes n algebraic equations in the n transforms.
Solve algebraically — solve the linear system for X(s), Y(s), … (by elimination or Cramer's rule), then invert each transform separately.
Initial conditions enter once — they appear in the algebraic system, so there is no second step of fixing constants.
The same idea, other methods — systems can also be solved by elimination (differentiate one equation and substitute) or by the eigenvalue method of the next lessons; Laplace is the most mechanical.

example.q: Solve x' = 2x + y, y' = x + 2y with x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0.
steps: Transform: sX − 1 = 2X + Y and sY = X + 2Y. From the second, X = (s − 2)Y.
Substitute into the first: s(s − 2)Y − 1 = 2(s − 2)Y + Y, giving (s² − 4s + 3)Y = 1, so Y = 1/((s − 1)(s − 3)) = (1/2)(1/(s − 3) − 1/(s − 1)).

practice.q: Solve x' = x, y' = 2y with x(0) = 1, y(0) = 2.
practice.a: x = e^t, y = 2e^{2t} (the equations are already uncoupled).

practice.q: Solve x' = y, y' = −x with x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0.
practice.a: x = cos t, y = −sin t.

lessons.takeaway: Transform every equation, solve the algebraic system for the transforms, invert each one — initial conditions are handled in one pass.

lessons.title: Review of Power Series
lessons.intro: When a differential equation resists closed-form methods, a power series can still solve it — but only if you know how series behave. This lesson is the toolkit: convergence, radius, and term-by-term calculus.
concepts: Power series — ∑ a_n (x − x0)ⁿ; it converges inside an interval around x0 and diverges outside, with radius R found by the ratio or root test.
Ratio test for R — R = 1 / lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| when the limit exists; for ∑ n xⁿ the ratio is (n+1)/n → 1, so R = 1.
Termwise differentiation — inside the interval of convergence, a power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term, and the radius stays the same: d/dx ∑ a_n xⁿ = ∑ n a_n x^{n−1}.
Key series — 1/(1 − x) = ∑ xⁿ, e^x = ∑ xⁿ/n!, sin x = ∑ (−1)ⁿ x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!, cos x = ∑ (−1)ⁿ x^{2n}/(2n)!; these are the benchmarks every series solution is compared against.

example.q: Find the radius of convergence of ∑ n xⁿ.
steps: Ratio test: |a_{n+1} x^{n+1} / (a_n xⁿ)| = ((n+1)/n) |x|.
As n → ∞, (n+1)/n → 1, so the ratio tends to |x|; the series converges when |x| < 1 and diverges when |x| > 1.
The radius of convergence is R = 1 (the endpoints x = ±1 diverge, since the terms do not go to zero).

practice.q: Find the radius of convergence of ∑ xⁿ/n².
Differentiate 1/(1 − x) = ∑ xⁿ term by term. What series do you get for 1/(1 − x)²?

lessons.takeaway: Series converge inside a radius found by the ratio test, and inside that interval you may differentiate and integrate term by term.

lessons.title: Series Solutions about Ordinary Points
lessons.intro: If x0 is an ordinary point of y'' + P(x) y' + Q(x) y = 0 — meaning P and Q are analytic there — then the equation has two power-series solutions about x0, and you find them by assuming y = ∑ a_n (x − x0)ⁿ and matching coefficients.
concepts: Ordinary point — P and Q have convergent power series at x0; for polynomial coefficients, every point where the leading coefficient is nonzero is ordinary.
The method — substitute y = ∑ a_n xⁿ (take x0 = 0 for simplicity), shift indices so every term is a multiple of xⁿ, and set each coefficient to zero to get a recurrence for a_n.
Two free constants — a_0 and a_1 are free (they are y(0) and y'(0)); the recurrence expresses every later a_n in terms of them, giving two independent series solutions.
Radius — the series converge at least up to the nearest singularity of P or Q in the complex plane.

example.q: Find the power-series solution of y'' + y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y'(0) = 0.
steps: Let y = ∑ a_n xⁿ. Then y'' = ∑ n(n − 1) a_n x^{n−2}; shifting the index, the coefficient of xⁿ in y'' + y = 0 is (n+2)(n+1) a_{n+2} + a_n.
Recurrence: a_{n+2} = −a_n / ((n+2)(n+1)). With a_0 = 1 and a_1 = 0, all odd coefficients vanish.

practice.q: Use series to solve y' − y = 0 with y(0) = 1.
practice.a: y = ∑ xⁿ/n! = e^x (recurrence a_{n+1} = a_n/(n+1)).

practice.q: For the Airy equation y'' − x y = 0, find a_3 and a_4 in terms of a_0 and a_1.

lessons.takeaway: Assume y = ∑ a_n xⁿ, shift indices, and the recurrence builds the solution from a_0 and a_1.

lessons.title: Series Solutions about Singular Points
lessons.intro: At a singular point the coefficients blow up and a plain power series may fail — the solution can have a logarithm or a fractional power. Frobenius's method fixes it: try y = x^r ∑ a_n xⁿ, and the indicial equation determines r.
concepts: Regular singular point — for x² y'' + x p(x) y' + q(x) y = 0 with p and q analytic at 0; the point x = 0 is regular singular (a pole of order at most 1 in P and 2 in Q).
Indicial equation — substituting y = x^r gives r(r − 1) + p(0) r + q(0) = 0; its roots r1, r2 are the possible leading exponents.
Distinct roots, no integer gap — each root gives a Frobenius series y = x^r ∑ a_n xⁿ, with a recurrence like the ordinary-point case.
Repeated root or integer gap — if r1 = r2, the second solution contains ln x; if r1 − r2 is a positive integer, the second solution may also need a logarithm.

example.q: Find the first three nonzero terms of a Frobenius series solution of Bessel's equation x² y'' + x y' + x² y = 0 about x = 0.
steps: Write it as x² y'' + x·1·y' + x²·y = 0: p(0) = 1, q(0) = 0, so the indicial equation is r(r − 1) + r = r² = 0, giving the double root r = 0.
With r = 0, try y = ∑ a_n xⁿ; the recurrence is a_n = −a_{n−2}/n² (odd coefficients vanish).
example.a: y1 = 1 − x²/4 + x⁴/64 − x⁶/2304 + ··· (times a constant)

practice.q: Find the indicial roots of x² y'' + 3x y' + y = 0.
practice.a: r = −1 (double root): r(r−1) + 3r + 1 = (r+1)² = 0.

practice.q: Find the indicial roots of x y'' + y' + x² y = 0.
practice.a: r = 0 (double root): r(r−1) + r = r² = 0.

lessons.takeaway: At a regular singular point, try y = x^r ∑ a_n xⁿ — the indicial equation picks r, and a repeated root or integer gap brings in ln x.

modules.module_title: Systems of Linear First-Order Differential Equations

lessons.title: Linear Systems
lessons.intro: A system of first-order linear equations is one equation in disguise: X' = A X + F(t), where X is a vector and A a matrix. Everything from the scalar theory — homogeneous and particular solutions, superposition — carries over, with matrices doing the bookkeeping.
concepts: Matrix form — the system x1' = a11 x1 + a12 x2 + f1, x2' = a21 x1 + a22 x2 + f2 becomes X' = AX + F with X = (x1, x2) and A the coefficient matrix.
Higher order to first order — an n-th order equation becomes a system of n first-order equations by setting x1 = y, x2 = y', …, xn = y^{(n−1)}; this is how computers solve ODEs.
Superposition — the general solution is X = X_h + X_p: a homogeneous part (a vector space of dimension n) plus any one particular solution.
Fundamental matrix — the columns of Φ(t) are n independent homogeneous solutions; every homogeneous solution is Φ(t) c for some constant vector c.

example.q: Write y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0 as a first-order system X' = AX.
steps: Set x1 = y and x2 = y'. Then x1' = x2 by definition.
From the equation, y'' = −2y − 3y', so x2' = −2x1 − 3x2.
In matrix form, X' = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] X.

practice.q: Write y''' − y = 0 as a first-order system.
Write the system x' = 2x − y, y' = x + y in the form X' = AX.

lessons.takeaway: A system is X' = AX + F; an n-th order equation becomes n first-order equations by naming each derivative a new variable.

lessons.title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
lessons.intro: For X' = AX with constant A, exponentials are again the key — but now they are vector exponentials. An eigenvalue λ with eigenvector v gives the solution e^{λt} v, and n independent eigenvectors span the whole solution space.
concepts: Eigenvalue solutions — if Av = λv with v ≠ 0, then X = e^{λt} v solves X' = AX; check it: X' = λ e^{λt} v = A e^{λt} v.
Distinct real eigenvalues — n distinct eigenvalues give n independent solutions e^{λ1 t} v1, …, e^{λn t} vn; the general solution is their combination.
Complex eigenvalues — λ = α ± βi gives a complex solution; its real and imaginary parts are two real solutions, and e^{αt}(cos βt, sin βt) combinations appear.
Repeated eigenvalues — a defective matrix (too few eigenvectors) needs generalized eigenvectors: solutions like t e^{λt} v appear, the matrix analogue of the repeated-root case.

steps: Eigenvalues: det(A − λI) = (1 − λ)² − 4 = 0, so λ = 3 and λ = −1.
General solution: X = C1 e^{3t} (1, 1) + C2 e^{−t} (1, −1).

practice.a: X = C1 (cos t, −sin t) + C2 (sin t, cos t).

lessons.takeaway: Eigenvalue λ with eigenvector v gives the solution e^{λt} v; n independent ones span the solution space.

lessons.title: Nonhomogeneous Linear Systems
lessons.intro: A forced system X' = AX + F(t) is solved the same way as a forced scalar equation: add a particular solution to the homogeneous general solution. Undetermined coefficients works when F is built from the usual families; variation of parameters, with the fundamental matrix, works always.
concepts: Undetermined coefficients for systems — if F(t) is a polynomial, exponential, or sinusoid (times a constant vector), guess a particular solution of the same shape; if it collides with a homogeneous solution, multiply by t.
Variation of parameters — with fundamental matrix Φ, seek X_p = Φ U; then U' = Φ^{−1} F, so U = ∫ Φ^{−1} F dt and X_p = Φ ∫ Φ^{−1} F dt.
Diagonal systems are easy — if A is diagonal, each equation is an independent scalar equation; the matrix methods are only needed when A couples the unknowns.
Steady states — for constant F, a constant particular solution X_p satisfies A X_p + F = 0; if A is invertible, X_p = −A^{−1} F.

example.q: Find a particular solution of X' = [[1, 0], [0, 2]] X + (e^t, 0).
steps: The fundamental matrix is Φ = diag(e^t, e^{2t}), so Φ^{−1} = diag(e^{−t}, e^{−2t}).
X_p = Φ U = (t e^t, 0). (Undetermined coefficients would also need the factor t, since e^t solves the homogeneous first equation.)

practice.q: Find a constant particular solution of X' = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] X + (0, 1).
Find a constant particular solution of X' = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] X + (1, 0).

lessons.takeaway: X = X_h + X_p: guess the forcing term's shape, or use X_p = Φ ∫ Φ^{−1} F dt for any forcing term.

lessons.title: Matrix Exponential
lessons.intro: The matrix exponential e^{At} is the fundamental matrix of X' = AX in closed form: the solution with X(0) = X0 is simply X(t) = e^{At} X0. It is defined by the same power series as the scalar exponential, and for the matrices you meet it has a closed form.
concepts: The definition — e^{At} = I + At + (At)²/2! + (At)³/3! + ···, which converges for every square matrix A.
The solution formula — X(t) = e^{At} X0 solves X' = AX with X(0) = X0; also d/dt e^{At} = A e^{At} = e^{At} A.
Diagonal matrices — if A = diag(λ1, …, λn), then e^{At} = diag(e^{λ1 t}, …, e^{λn t}).

Computing it — diagonalize A = PDP^{−1} and use e^{At} = P e^{Dt} P^{−1}; for a rotation matrix [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] the series collapses to [[cos t, sin t], [−sin t, cos t]]; for A = I + N with N² = 0, e^{At} = e^t (I + tN).

example.q: Compute e^{At} for A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] and use it to solve X' = AX with X(0) = (1, 1).
steps: A is diagonal, so e^{At} = diag(e^{2t}, e^{3t}).
Check: x' = 2e^{2t} = 2x and y' = 3e^{3t} = 3y.

practice.q: Compute e^{At} for A = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]].
practice.a: [[cos t, sin t], [−sin t, cos t]] (the series gives the rotation matrix).

practice.q: Compute e^{At} for A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]].
practice.a: e^t [[1, t], [0, 1]] (A = I + N with N² = 0, so e^{At} = e^t (I + tN)).

lessons.takeaway: e^{At} is the fundamental matrix: X(t) = e^{At} X0 solves the system, and diagonal or rotation matrices give it in closed form.

MATH202.mastery_rubric: To pass, students must be able to solve various types of first- and second-order differential equations, apply Laplace transforms, and find series solutions. A clear understanding of modeling real-world phenomena with differential equations is crucial. Final course grade must be 70% or higher, with at least 60% on the final exam.

modules.module_title: Systems of Linear Equations and Matrices

lessons.title: Introduction to Systems of Linear Equations
lessons.intro: A system of linear equations is a collection of equations in which every unknown appears only to the first power. Such systems are everywhere — balancing chemical reactions, solving circuits, fitting data — and the whole course grows out of one question: how do we find all the solutions, efficiently and reliably?
concepts: Linear equation — an equation of the form a1x1 + a2x2 + … + anxn = b, where the ai and b are constants and each unknown appears to the first power; x + 2y − z = 4 is linear, xy = 1 is not.
Solution — an assignment of numbers to the unknowns that makes every equation in the system true at once; a system can have exactly one solution, infinitely many, or none at all.
Consistent vs. inconsistent — a system is consistent if it has at least one solution and inconsistent if it has none; two parallel lines give an inconsistent 2×2 system.
Geometric picture — in two unknowns each equation is a line: one solution means the lines cross, infinitely many means they are the same line, none means they are parallel.

Equivalent systems — two systems with the same solution set; the elementary operations (swap equations, multiply an equation by a nonzero constant, add a multiple of one equation to another) produce equivalent systems, which is why elimination works.

example.q: Solve the system x + y = 5, x − y = 1, and check the answer.
steps: Add the equations: (x + y) + (x − y) = 5 + 1, so 2x = 6 and x = 3.
Substitute back: 3 + y = 5, so y = 2.
Check: 3 + 2 = 5 ✓ and 3 − 2 = 1 ✓, so (3, 2) satisfies both equations.

practice.q: Solve 2x + y = 7, x − y = 2.
practice.a: Adding gives 3x = 9, so x = 3; then y = 1. Check: 2·3 + 1 = 7 ✓, 3 − 1 = 2 ✓.

practice.q: Solve x + 2y = 8, 3x − y = 1.
practice.a: From the second equation y = 3x − 1; then x + 2(3x − 1) = 8 gives 7x = 10, so x = 10/7 and y = 23/7.

lessons.takeaway: A linear system has one, infinitely many, or no solutions; elimination by combining equations preserves the solution set while simplifying it.

lessons.title: Gaussian Elimination
lessons.intro: Gaussian elimination is the systematic way to solve any linear system: turn it into a triangular system by row operations, then read the answers off from the bottom up. It is the algorithm behind every computer solve of Ax = b, and it also tells you when a system has no solution or infinitely many.
concepts: Augmented matrix — the coefficient matrix with the right-hand sides appended as an extra column; row operations on the matrix are exactly the equation operations that preserve solutions.
Row-echelon form — a matrix where each leading entry (pivot) sits to the right of the pivot above it and all-zero rows are at the bottom; a system in this form is solved by back-substitution.
Reduced row-echelon form — row-echelon form with every pivot equal to 1 and zeros above each pivot too; the solution can then be read off directly.
Free variables — variables with no pivot column; each free variable can take any value, giving infinitely many solutions, one per choice of the free variables.
Inconsistency test — a row [0 0 … 0 | b] with b ≠ 0 in the reduced matrix means 0 = b, so the system has no solution.

example.q: Use Gaussian elimination to solve x + 2y + z = 4, 2x + y − z = 1, x − y + 2z = 3.
steps: Check in the second equation: 2(5/6) + 5/6 − 3/2 = 10/6 + 5/6 − 9/6 = 1 ✓.

practice.q: Solve x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 by elimination.
practice.a: Adding gives 3x = 3, so x = 1; then y = 2.

practice.q: Show that x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 5 has no solution.
practice.a: Doubling the first equation gives 2x + 2y = 2, contradicting 2x + 2y = 5; elimination produces the row [0 0 | 3], so the system is inconsistent.

lessons.takeaway: Row operations reduce any system to triangular form; pivots mark the determined variables, free variables mark the choices, and a 0 = b row marks inconsistency.

lessons.title: Matrices and Matrix Operations
lessons.intro: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, and the real power of linear algebra comes from treating whole arrays as single objects that can be added and multiplied. Matrix multiplication looks strange at first — it is not entry-by-entry — but it is exactly the rule that makes matrices represent systems and transformations.
concepts: Matrix — an m×n array with m rows and n columns; the (i, j)-entry sits in row i, column j; a vector is a matrix with one column.
Addition and scalar multiplication — entry-by-entry: (A + B)ij = Aij + Bij and (cA)ij = c·Aij; addition requires the same size.
Matrix multiplication — (AB)ij is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, so AB needs A's column count to equal B's row count; an m×n times an n×p matrix is m×p.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative — in general AB ≠ BA, and both products may not even exist; order matters, always.
Transpose — Aᵀ flips rows and columns, (Aᵀ)ij = Aji; (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ, with the order reversed.

example.q: For A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[0, 1], [−1, 2]], compute AB and BA.
steps: AB ≠ BA, as expected: matrix multiplication is not commutative.

practice.q: For A and B above, compute A + B, A − B, and 2A.
Can you multiply a 2×3 matrix by a 2×2 matrix? What about a 3×2 matrix by a 2×2 matrix?
practice.a: No for the first (3 ≠ 2, inner dimensions mismatch); yes for the second, giving a 3×2 matrix.

lessons.takeaway: Matrix multiplication is row-times-column, not entry-times-entry; sizes must match inside, and order matters — AB and BA are usually different.

lessons.title: Inverses; Rules of Matrix Arithmetic
lessons.intro: The inverse of a square matrix A is the matrix A⁻¹ that undoes it: A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I. Inverses turn the problem 'solve Ax = b' into a single multiplication, x = A⁻¹b — when an inverse exists. Not every matrix has one, and the arithmetic rules (like (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹) mirror the transpose rules with the same order reversal.
concepts: Inverse matrix — for square A, A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I; if it exists it is unique, and A is then called invertible or nonsingular.
2×2 inverse formula — for A = [[a, b], [c, d]] with ad − bc ≠ 0, A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]]; the number ad − bc is the determinant.
Solving with an inverse — if A is invertible, Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b; if A is not invertible, Ax = b may have no solution or infinitely many.
Singular matrices — a square matrix with no inverse is singular; for 2×2 this happens exactly when ad − bc = 0, i.e. when one row is a multiple of the other.
Inverse of a product — (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, order reversed, just like the transpose rule (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; also (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A and (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ.

example.q: Find the inverse of A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] and use it to solve Ax = [3, 2]ᵀ.
steps: Determinant: det A = 2·1 − 1·1 = 1 ≠ 0, so A is invertible.
