practice.a: Because children in single-parent, blended, or two-parent homes do better when the family has stable income, time, and support — and worse when it does not, regardless of the form.

lessons.takeaway: Families are changing form faster than function — the real question is whether care, stability, and support still reach the children.

lessons.title: Education and Inequality of Opportunity
lessons.intro: School is supposed to be the great equalizer — the place where talent, not birth, decides your future. The data tells a more complicated story: children from wealthy families are far more likely to graduate, attend selective colleges, and land high-paying jobs. Education opens doors, but it also reproduces the inequality it is meant to erase.
concepts: The promise and the reality — schools teach skills and certify ability, but they also sort students. The sorting is not neutral: it tracks family income, neighborhood, and race.

Cultural capital — Pierre Bourdieu: the unspoken knowledge of the educated class (how to talk to a teacher, what to put on an application, which books matter). Schools reward it without teaching it, so children who arrive with it look 'naturally' gifted.
Tracking — sorting students into ability groups or tracks. It can help advanced students, but it often locks lower-track students into lower expectations, weaker teaching, and less learning.

Funding gaps — American schools are funded largely by local property taxes, so rich neighborhoods have rich schools and poor neighborhoods have poor ones. The zip code a child is born in predicts the school they attend.

Credentialism — the growing demand for degrees as a ticket to jobs that once needed none. When everyone needs a degree, the degree itself becomes a gate, and the gate is hardest for those with the least money.

example.q: Two students with identical test scores apply to the same selective college. One's parents hired an admissions consultant and paid for three SAT attempts; the other is the first in her family to apply and did it alone. The first is admitted, the second is not. Is this meritocracy?
steps: On paper, the process is merit-based: same scores, one decision. In practice, the inputs were unequal — coaching, retakes, and insider knowledge about what the application should look like.
Cultural capital explains the gap: the first student knew the unspoken rules (which essay topic works, how to frame an activity) because her family already knew them.
Tracking and funding add up earlier: the two students likely attended different schools with different resources long before the application.
Conclusion: education can reward talent, but when preparation is bought, the result measures family resources as much as student ability.

practice.q: What is cultural capital?
practice.a: The unspoken knowledge, tastes, and manners of the educated class that schools reward but do not teach — like how to speak to authority, what counts as a good essay, or which activities impress admissions.

practice.q: How does local school funding create inequality?
practice.a: Schools funded by local property taxes get more money in wealthy areas, so children in rich neighborhoods attend better-funded schools with smaller classes and more resources than children in poor ones.

lessons.takeaway: Education promises equal opportunity but often reproduces inequality — because preparation, funding, and unspoken rules are not equally distributed.

lessons.title: Religion in Society
lessons.intro: Religion is one of humanity's oldest institutions — and one of the most argued about. It comforts the grieving, binds communities, and inspires charity; it has also justified wars, defended slavery, and resisted change. Sociology does not ask whether a religion is true. It asks what religion does: how it holds groups together, how it changes, and why it persists in a scientific age.
concepts: Durkheim on religion — religion is society worshipping itself: shared rituals and sacred symbols create solidarity. The sacred is whatever a group sets apart and treats with reverence, whether it is a god, a flag, or a text.
Weber on religion — ideas matter: Weber argued that Protestant ethics (hard work, thrift, calling) helped create modern capitalism. Beliefs can change economies, not just reflect them.

Marx on religion — religion is the 'opium of the people': it soothes suffering in this world while distracting from the causes of that suffering. For Marx, it serves the powerful by making inequality feel divinely ordained.

Secularization — the long decline of religious authority in public life in many Western countries. It is uneven: the US remains far more religious than Western Europe, and religion is growing in much of the world.

Religious markets — in countries with many competing faiths, religions behave like firms competing for members, often becoming more energetic and participatory. Monopolies breed complacency; competition breeds effort.

example.q: A small town's annual religious festival draws the whole community — believers and non-believers alike — for food, music, and a parade. A sociologist calls the festival important even for people who do not believe. Why?
steps: Durkheim's answer: the festival's real function is solidarity. Shared ritual — eating together, marching together — binds the community whether or not anyone believes the theology.
The sacred here is the community itself: the parade route, the old church, the shared meal are set apart and treated with reverence by everyone.
Even the non-believers participate in the ritual, which means the social function (belonging) works independently of the belief function (faith).
Conclusion: religion's social power is not only in what people believe, but in what they do together — and that is why festivals outlast faith in many places.

practice.q: What did Durkheim mean when he said religion is society worshipping itself?
practice.a: Religious rituals and sacred symbols create group solidarity — the community's shared reverence binds people together, and the 'sacred' is whatever the group sets apart.

practice.q: How does secularization differ between the US and Western Europe?
practice.a: Western Europe has seen a steep decline in church attendance and religious authority, while the US remains much more religious — showing secularization is uneven, not universal.

lessons.takeaway: Sociology studies what religion does — binding communities, shaping economies, soothing or legitimizing — not whether its claims are true.

lessons.title: Government, Power and the Economy
lessons.intro: Who rules, who decides, and who gets what — these are the questions of political sociology and economic sociology, and they are inseparable. Governments set the rules of the economy, economies fund governments, and power flows through both. The key sociological insight is that power is not only in laws and armies: it is also in who gets to define what counts as a problem.
concepts: Power and authority — power is the ability to get others to do what you want; authority is power that people accept as legitimate. Weber's three types: traditional (a king), charismatic (a revolutionary leader), and rational-legal (a constitution).
The state — the institution with a monopoly on legitimate force in a territory. It makes laws, collects taxes, and enforces order — and its form (democracy, authoritarianism) shapes everything else.

Pluralism vs power elite — pluralists say power is spread among many competing groups; power-elite theorists (C. Wright Mills) say a small interlocking elite of political, military, and corporate leaders makes the big decisions.
The economy as a social institution — markets are not natural laws; they are built on laws, trust, norms, and networks. What can be bought and sold, and by whom, is a social decision.
Welfare and the state — modern states redistribute income through taxes, schools, healthcare, and pensions. How much they redistribute is one of the biggest political divides in any society.

example.q: A city council votes to rezone a poor neighborhood for luxury apartments. Residents protest that they were never consulted; developers say the project brings jobs and tax revenue. Analyze the conflict with two theories of power.
steps: Pluralism would look for the competition: residents, developers, and the council all have a voice, and the outcome depends on who organizes best and who shows up.
Power-elite theory would look for the connections: developers who fund campaigns, council members who later join development firms, and a process where residents' protests are heard but not heeded.
The sociological question is not just who won the vote, but who set the agenda: who decided rezoning was the issue, and who decided that 'jobs and tax revenue' was the frame?
Conclusion: both theories may be partly right — pluralism explains the open contest, power-elite theory explains why the contest is rarely equal.

practice.q: What is the difference between power and authority?
practice.a: Power is the ability to get others to act as you wish, even against resistance; authority is power that people accept as legitimate — they obey because they believe they should.

practice.q: Why do sociologists say markets are social institutions?
practice.a: Because markets depend on laws, trust, norms, and networks — what can be bought, who can trade, and how contracts are enforced are all social arrangements, not laws of nature.

lessons.takeaway: Power is not only force — it is legitimate authority, agenda-setting, and the rules that decide who gets what.

lessons.title: Health, Medicine and Society
lessons.intro: Illness feels private — your body, your pain. But who gets sick, who gets treated, and who dies young are profoundly social facts. The same disease kills the poor far more often than the rich, in every country and every era. The sociology of health asks why, and what medicine — itself a powerful institution — does about it.
concepts: The social gradient of health — health improves step by step with income and education, not just between rich and poor but at every rung of the ladder. Stress, housing, food, and safety explain most of the gap.

The sick role — Talcott Parsons: when you are sick, society excuses you from normal duties — but expects you to want to get better and to seek proper help. The role is a bargain between the patient and society.

Medicalization — turning human problems into medical ones: shyness becomes social anxiety disorder, restlessness becomes ADHD. Medicalization brings treatment, but also labels and drugs where social change might help.

Health inequality — race, gender, and class shape access to care, quality of care, and outcomes. Black Americans, for example, face higher maternal mortality than white Americans at every income level.

Medicine as an institution — doctors hold enormous authority (the power to define illness, prescribe, and certify). That authority helps patients, but it can also silence them — which is why patient advocacy and second opinions matter.

example.q: Two neighborhoods in the same city have a 15-year gap in life expectancy. The richer one has grocery stores and parks; the poorer one has fast food, a highway, and a closed clinic. A doctor says the gap is because poor people make bad health choices. What is the sociological response?
steps: The gradient is the clue: a 15-year gap is too large to be explained by individual choices alone — it points to conditions, not character.
Check the environment: fresh food, safe places to walk, clean air, and a clinic are not choices the residents made — they are features of the neighborhood that shape every choice.
Chronic stress matters: living with noise, danger, and financial insecurity keeps the body's stress system switched on, which damages health over years.
Conclusion: choices matter, but choices are made inside conditions. Fix the conditions — food access, safety, care — and the choices change with them.

practice.q: What is the sick role?
practice.a: Parsons' idea that a sick person is excused from normal duties but is expected to want to recover and to seek competent medical help — a social bargain, not just a biological state.

practice.q: What is medicalization, and why is it controversial?
practice.a: Defining a human problem as a medical condition. It brings treatment and legitimacy, but it can also turn social or normal problems into diseases that need drugs instead of social change.

lessons.takeaway: Health is social: the same disease strikes differently by class, race, and neighborhood — because conditions, not just choices, decide who gets sick.

lessons.title: Social Stratification and Class
lessons.intro: Every society ranks its members — by wealth, by power, by prestige — and the ranking shapes almost everything: where you live, how long you live, who you marry, and what your children can become. Stratification is the system that produces those ranks. The question is not whether ranking exists, but how open or closed it is, and what it does to the people at the bottom.
concepts: Class systems vs caste — a class system allows movement (you can rise or fall); a caste system fixes your rank at birth. Most modern societies are class systems, but movement is harder than the myth suggests.
Wealth vs income — income is what you earn in a year; wealth is what you own. Wealth is far more unequal than income, and it is what really buys security, education, and opportunity.
Status and prestige — not all ranking is about money: a teacher may earn less than a plumber but hold higher prestige. Wealth, power, and prestige usually overlap but can come apart.

Social mobility — movement up or down the ladder. Intergenerational mobility compares children to their parents; structural mobility happens when the economy itself changes (new industries create new middle-class jobs).
The poverty trap — poverty is not just low income: it is the package of unstable housing, poor schools, expensive credit, and constant stress that makes escaping harder the longer you are in it.

example.q: A janitor's daughter and a surgeon's daughter both graduate from the same high school with the same grades. Ten years later, one is a manager and the other is still in low-wage work. A friend says the manager just worked harder. What does stratification theory say?
steps: Start with wealth, not income: the surgeon's family could fund unpaid internships, a car, and a move to a job-rich city; the janitor's daughter could not afford to work for free.
Add networks: the surgeon's daughter grew up meeting professionals; the janitor's daughter's network is mostly low-wage workers. Jobs come through contacts as often as through applications.
Add cultural capital: knowing how to interview, how to dress, how to talk to a boss — all learned at home, all rewarded at work, none of it taught in school.
Conclusion: effort matters, but it operates on an uneven field. Mobility exists, but the odds are stacked by the resources a family can pass on.

practice.q: Why is wealth more important than income for understanding inequality?
practice.a: Wealth is accumulated assets — it buys security, education, and opportunity, cushions crises, and is passed to children; income stops when the paycheck stops.

practice.q: What is the difference between intergenerational and structural mobility?
practice.a: Intergenerational mobility is a child's rank compared with their parents'; structural mobility is change caused by the economy itself, like new industries creating middle-class jobs.

lessons.takeaway: Stratification ranks everyone by wealth, power, and prestige — and the resources your family can pass on shape your odds more than effort alone.

lessons.title: Race and Ethnicity
lessons.intro: Race is one of the most powerful forces in social life — and biologically, it is almost meaningless. Human genetic variation does not line up with racial categories; the categories are social inventions. But the consequences are brutally real: race shapes where you live, how you are treated by police and employers, and how long you live. Sociology studies race as a social construction with real effects.
concepts: Race as a social construction — racial categories were invented to justify slavery and colonialism, and they change over time and place: the same person can be 'white' in one country and not in another, and the US census categories have changed repeatedly.

Ethnicity vs race — ethnicity is shared culture, language, and ancestry (Irish, Mexican, Korean); race is a category imposed largely by physical appearance and social definition. A person can share an ethnicity with people of different races.

Prejudice vs discrimination — prejudice is an attitude (a belief about a group); discrimination is an action (treating someone differently). You can be prejudiced without discriminating, and you can discriminate without personal prejudice, through rules that hit one group harder.

Institutional racism — patterns built into institutions: redlining that denied mortgages to Black neighborhoods, school funding tied to property taxes, hiring that runs through segregated networks. No single bigot is required for the pattern to persist.

Intersectionality — Kimberle Crenshaw: race, gender, and class do not act separately. A Black woman faces a different combination of barriers than a Black man or a white woman, and the effects multiply.

example.q: A company says it hires purely on merit and never considers race. Yet its workforce is 90% white in a city that is 50% white, because it hires mainly through employee referrals. Is this discrimination?
steps: No individual hiring manager needs to be prejudiced for this outcome to happen: the referral system reproduces the existing workforce, which is the definition of an institutional pattern.
The mechanism is network segregation: people's friends and family tend to share their race, so a referral system quietly favors the majority group without ever mentioning race.
This is discrimination in effect, not in intent — sociologists call it institutional discrimination, and it persists precisely because nobody feels responsible for it.
Fix: change the structure — open applications, blind resume review, outreach to underrepresented communities — not just the attitudes.

practice.q: Why do sociologists say race is a social construction?
practice.a: Because racial categories were created by societies, change across time and place, and do not match biological genetic variation — yet they have very real social consequences.

practice.q: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
practice.a: Prejudice is an attitude or belief about a group; discrimination is acting on it — treating people differently because of their group membership.

lessons.takeaway: Race is invented by society but real in its effects — and much of its power works through institutions, not just individual attitudes.

lessons.title: Gender and Society
lessons.intro: Sex is biological; gender is what society does with it. From the moment a baby is wrapped in pink or blue, the world starts teaching what it means to be a girl or a boy — what to play with, how to speak, what jobs to want. Gender shapes pay, power, safety, and everyday life, and it is enforced by rewards for fitting in and penalties for stepping out.
concepts: Sex vs gender — sex refers to biological differences; gender refers to the social roles, behaviors, and expectations attached to being male, female, or nonbinary. Gender varies across cultures and history.
Gender socialization — children learn gender from family, school, peers, and media: toys, clothes, praise for being 'tough' or 'nice.' The lessons are so early and constant they feel natural.

The gender pay gap — women earn about 80 cents for every dollar men earn in the US. Part is occupational segregation (women concentrated in lower-paid fields); part is the motherhood penalty; part is outright discrimination.

The glass ceiling and the glass escalator — women face invisible barriers to top jobs (the ceiling); men in female-dominated fields are often promoted faster than their female colleagues (the escalator).

Doing gender — Candace West: gender is not something you are but something you do, performed in everyday interaction. Because it is performed, it can be performed differently — which is how change happens.

example.q: A hospital's nursing staff is 90% women. A male nurse is promoted to supervisor after two years, faster than female nurses with five years of experience. The manager says he was simply the best candidate. What does sociology see here?
steps: The glass escalator: men in female-dominated professions are often fast-tracked into leadership, while women in male-dominated fields face the opposite — the glass ceiling.
The mechanism is partly stereotype: leadership is culturally coded as masculine, so a man in a caring profession is read as 'management material' while women are read as 'natural carers.'
Occupational segregation set the stage: nursing is undervalued partly because it is coded as women's work, which holds down pay for everyone in it.
Conclusion: individual merit is real, but it is judged through a gendered lens. The pattern across many hospitals, not one promotion, is the evidence.

practice.q: What is the difference between sex and gender?
practice.a: Sex is biological (chromosomes, anatomy); gender is the social roles, expectations, and behaviors a society attaches to being male, female, or nonbinary.

practice.q: What is occupational segregation, and how does it feed the pay gap?
practice.a: The concentration of women in lower-paid fields (care, teaching, service) and men in higher-paid ones (engineering, finance). Because 'women's work' is paid less, segregation itself lowers women's average pay.

lessons.takeaway: Gender is learned, performed, and enforced — and it structures pay, promotion, and power in ways that look personal but are patterned.

lessons.title: Global Stratification
lessons.intro: Inequality does not stop at national borders. The gap between the richest and poorest countries is wider than the gap between the richest and poorest people inside most countries. A child born in one country can expect 80 years of life; a child born in another, 55. Global stratification asks why whole nations are rich or poor — and whether the system itself keeps them that way.
concepts: Core, semi-periphery, periphery — world-systems theory (Immanuel Wallerstein): wealthy core nations dominate trade and finance; semi-peripheral nations manufacture and struggle upward; peripheral nations supply raw materials and cheap labor, and stay poor.

Colonialism's legacy — many poor nations were colonies whose economies were built to export raw materials to Europe. Independence changed the flag, not the economic structure — and the debts and borders left behind still shape them.

Modernization theory — the older view that poor nations are simply 'behind' and will develop by following the rich nations' path: industrialize, educate, urbanize. Critics say it blames the victim and ignores exploitation.

Dependency theory — the counter-view: poor nations are poor because the global system extracts value from them — cheap labor, raw materials, debt payments — and transfers it to the core. Development requires changing the rules, not just working harder.

Globalization's double edge — trade and technology have lifted hundreds of millions out of extreme poverty, but the gains are uneven: factory workers in one country gain jobs while workers in another lose them, and the profits concentrate at the top.

example.q: A country exports raw cocoa beans for a few cents a pound; a company in a rich country turns them into chocolate bars sold for dollars. The cocoa country stays poor despite growing more cocoa every year. Which theory explains this best?
steps: Dependency theory fits: the cocoa country is in the periphery, supplying raw materials while the core captures the value by processing, branding, and selling the finished product.

Modernization theory would say the country should industrialize and move up the chain — build its own chocolate factories — which is correct as advice but ignores the barriers: capital, trade rules, and debt.
World-systems theory adds the structure: the global division of labor assigns the low-profit stage to the periphery, and moving up requires fighting the rules that keep it there.
Conclusion: growing more of the same raw material will not close the gap. The question is who controls the profitable stages of production.

practice.q: In world-systems theory, what distinguishes core nations from peripheral ones?
practice.a: Core nations dominate high-profit manufacturing, finance, and technology; peripheral nations supply raw materials and cheap labor and capture little of the value.

practice.q: Why do dependency theorists criticize modernization theory?
practice.a: Because it treats poor nations as merely 'behind' and blames their culture or effort, while ignoring how the global system extracts value from them to the core.

lessons.takeaway: Global inequality is a system, not a scoreboard — core nations capture the value, peripheral nations supply the raw material, and history set the rules.

lessons.title: Social Movements and Social Change
lessons.intro: Societies do not only change slowly — sometimes they change because ordinary people organize and demand it. The civil rights movement, the women's suffrage movement, the labor movement: none of them were inevitable, and none of them were the work of a single hero. Social movements are how people who lack power in institutions create power together.
concepts: What makes a movement — a shared grievance, a sense of injustice, organization, and resources. Grievance alone is not enough: people have been angry for centuries without a movement forming.

Resource mobilization — movements succeed when they gather money, people, media attention, and allies. The civil rights movement had churches, lawyers, and national media; that infrastructure was the engine.
Political opportunity — movements win when the system opens: a sympathetic court, a divided elite, an election year. Timing matters as much as passion.

Framing — how a movement names the problem decides who joins. 'Civil rights' framed segregation as a constitutional issue; 'states' rights' framed the same conflict as federal overreach. The frame is the fight.

Outcomes and backlash — movements change laws, norms, and lives, but success often triggers backlash: new rules, new resistance, new movements in the other direction. Change is a process, not a finish line.

example.q: For decades, a city's bus system required Black riders to sit at the back. Then, within a year, the rule was gone. A textbook says 'attitudes changed.' Why is that explanation incomplete?
steps: Attitudes alone do not change laws: people had disliked the rule for decades. What changed was organization — a boycott that lasted over a year, with carpools, churches, and donations sustaining it.
Resource mobilization: the boycott had money, leaders, lawyers, and national press. Without those resources, the grievance stayed private.
Political opportunity: a court case and a divided political establishment opened a window, and the movement was ready when it opened.
Conclusion: social change needs grievance plus organization plus opportunity. 'Attitudes changed' is the story told afterward; the movement is what made it happen.

practice.q: Why is grievance alone not enough to create a social movement?
practice.a: Because many people feel aggrieved without organizing; a movement also needs resources, organization, allies, and a political opening to act on the grievance.

practice.q: What is framing, and why does it matter?
practice.a: How a movement names and explains a problem. The frame decides who sees the issue as theirs, who joins, and what solutions seem reasonable.

lessons.takeaway: Change is organized: grievance plus resources plus an opening — movements are how people without institutional power make it.

lessons.title: Final Project: A Sociological Look at Your Own Community
lessons.intro: This course ends where sociology begins: with your own eyes. Your final project is a small study of your own community — a neighborhood, a workplace, a campus, a family — using the tools of the course. Pick one question, gather real evidence, and explain what you find with theory. You are not writing a report about sociology; you are doing it.
concepts: Pick a question you can actually answer — 'Why do people in my building never talk to each other?' is answerable; 'Why is society unfair?' is not. A good question is small, specific, and observable.

Use the three lenses — analyze your findings with functionalism (what holds this group together?), conflict theory (who benefits?), and interactionism (what do things mean here?). A project that uses all three is stronger than one that uses one.
Gather evidence honestly — observe for a week and keep notes, run a short survey of ten people, or interview three neighbors. Record what people actually say and do, not what you expected.
Mind the ethics — tell people you are observing or interviewing them for a class project, keep names out of the final write-up, and do not study anyone in a way that could harm them.
Write it like a sociologist — describe the pattern, name the concepts that explain it, admit what your evidence cannot prove, and end with one thing you would change and how.

example.q: A student studies her apartment building: nobody uses the shared laundry room after 6pm, though the rules allow it until 10pm. She interviews three neighbors and finds they are afraid of one man who loiters there in the evenings. What is the sociological story?
steps: The pattern is real and observable: an empty room after 6pm is a social fact, not a coincidence.
Interactionism: the laundry room means 'unsafe' to residents after dark, even though nothing has happened there — the meaning drives the behavior.
Conflict theory: one person's behavior controls a shared resource, and the people with the least power (renters, women, older residents) pay the cost by changing their routines.
Functionalism asks what the pattern does: it keeps the peace by avoiding confrontation, but at the cost of the residents' use of a space they pay for.
Conclusion: a small observation, read through three lenses, becomes a real sociological finding — and it points to a fix (lighting, a lock, a schedule) rather than just a complaint.

practice.q: Why is a small, specific question better than a big, general one for this project?
practice.a: Because a small question can be answered with real evidence you can gather in a week — observation, a few interviews, a short survey — while a big question needs data you cannot collect.

practice.q: What must you do ethically when interviewing neighbors for your project?
practice.a: Tell them it is for a class project, get their agreement, keep their names out of the write-up, and avoid questions or observations that could embarrass or harm them.

lessons.takeaway: Sociology is a way of seeing: ask a small question, gather real evidence, read it through the three lenses, and say what you found.
